The Yogaśikhā Upaniṣad.
"May He protect us both"—this is the Peace.
Chapter One.
A desire to know the path to liberation:
All living beings are enveloped by the net of illusion consisting of pleasures and pains.
O Lord Śaṅkara, tell me out of compassion: how may their liberation be attained? (1)
Speak of the path that brings about all accomplishments, which cuts through the net of illusion,
destroys birth, death, old age, and disease, and bestows happiness.
Thus [it is said].
In the commentary on the knowledge of Yoga, which is renowned as the means for attaining that state,
that reality of Brahman consisting of three words remains as one's own self alone.

Herein indeed, this Yogaśikhā Upaniṣad, which is a branch of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, stands preeminent, intent upon revealing the entire essence of the yoga of knowledge along with its means, and resting solely in Brahman. A commentary on this [text], though brief in its wording, is now begun. [The relationship of] disciple and teacher—
This is for the purpose of praising knowledge. First, he introduces the narrative with the words "All... (1). To the question "What is that?", he replies with "All... (2).
(391) Hiraṇyagarbha asked about the difficulty of attaining the path to liberation; Maheśvara spoke thus:
"The supreme state of absolute isolation (kaivalya) is difficult to reach even by means of various paths."
One attains it by the path of accomplishment (siddhimārga) and not otherwise, O Padmasambhava.
For the sake of benefiting the world, Hiraṇyagarbha questioned Maheśvara. Having accepted that question, he spoke. Regarding what he said, the meaning will be stated hereafter.

He praises [the Lord] by illuminating [this truth]: "Not another" (nānya). Because [He] is accessible solely through non-dual knowledge devoid of distinctions. By the path of established perfection proven by the scripture, "There exists no other path for going," this path which bestows the attainment of liberation (*kaivalya*) consists in the knowledge of Brahman alone as devoid of distinctions; by that very [path].
The meaning is that one attains isolation (kaivalya) and not otherwise.
Brahman is accessible only through the scriptures; yet they have fallen into the snares of the scriptures, deluded by their own intellect. || 4 ||
Since that [reality] is of the nature of the self-luminous, how could it be illuminated by a scripture?
It is partless, stainless, tranquil, transcending all, and free from affliction.
That very same eternal state of the Supreme Self, when enveloped by the fruits of merit and demerit in the form of the individual soul (jīva), how did it come to attain the condition of being a jīva?
O Mahādeva, O Īśvara, by Your grace I shall speak of that which transcends the [lower] principles (*tattva*).
It mocks those who have strayed onto wrong paths and possess only semblance-knowledge (*ābhāsajñāna*), calling them "fallen"— those who,
having forgotten the four means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and residence in the teacher’s house (*gurukula-vāsa*), [rely only on] the three Tantras.

"Has the *Turyatantra* been studied by me? Has it not been studied?"—such [questions] are rendered futile by the sight of its true nature, because Brahman, having dispelled the meaning of words and sentences, is self-luminous by its very essence; for it is that which makes the knower aware of the meaningful, rather than being made known by them.

Regarding the question of what kind of Brahman is that which has the nature of the self-luminous light—[the text says] "partless" (*niṣkala*). The meaning is that Brahman, established through the negation (*apahnava*) of the sixteen parts (*kalā*) beginning with *prāṇa* and ending with *nāman*, is the non-dual partless Brahman alone. || 5 || Of the partless [Brahman]...

Since the multitude of living beings might be thought distinct from that which is pure Brahman, he says: "That very same [Brahman]. That which remains as its own essence alone from the perspective of one who knows itself (svajña), is that very same thing from the perspective of one ignorant of itself (svājña). He raises an objection—asking how the Supreme Self can assume the state of being a living being—with the words: "The Supreme Self... (verse 6). That.
Of what nature? Beyond reality.
The state of being a living soul (jīva) of Brahman is stainless, consisting of pure knowledge, and transcends all states of existence.
Like the wind, a vibration arose within itself, and from that, the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti) emerged;
it became a body composed of the five elements, bound by the constituents and consisting of the qualities (guṇas).
Regard that which is joined with pleasure and pain as the "living being" (jīva);
by that [designation], the name "jīva" is applied to the pure Supreme Self (paramātman).

To this question, the Blessed One replied: "All," [verse 7]. That very same [reality], from the perspective of one who does not know themselves, appears like wind in the sky. From its presence, the body consisting of the five elements arose.
That which remains as nothing but one's own non-dual nature is, from the perspective of one who knows themselves and so forth, something slight.
That which has manifested assumes the state of being a witness. The manifestation as the three-quarters (tripāda-bhūti) alone shines forth as eternal manifestation (nitya-bhūti).

That very eternal manifestation, having attained the state of the perfect "I" (pūrṇāhaṃbhāva), becomes playful manifestation (līlā-bhūti). Even that playful manifestation, due to the identification with limited bodies, becomes delusive manifestation (moha-bhūti). And that too, in the form of the body and so forth...
The meaning is that Jaḍabhūti also becomes [one with the Self]. || 8-9 ||
The state of Śiva belongs to the living being who is liberated from defects such as desire:
desire, anger, fear, delusion, greed, and passion (rajas);
as well as birth, death, wretchedness, grief, drowsiness, hunger, and thirst. (10)
Thirst, shame, fear, suffering, despondency, and even joy—one liberated from these defects is called that living being, Śiva. (11)
It has been stated that one who possesses only three quarters, due to the conceit of identifying with the limited body, partakes in the state of being a "deluded being" (mohabhūti).

To the question of how such a deluded being can attain the state of being a "playful being" (līlādibhūti) and so forth, it is said: through the awakening "I am the three-quarters," at the very moment one abandons the mental fluctuations of desire and the like rooted in the conceit of the body and so forth, there arises precisely the state of being the three-quarters.

To this he says: "In desire," etc. (10). This fault consists in the inclusion of the fluctuations of desire and so forth, because the manifestation of the three qualities leads to the manifestation of delusion. (11)
The destruction of defects occurs through the practice of knowledge and yoga;
therefore, for the sake of destroying those defects, I shall tell you the means.
Some say that in this matter, knowledge alone is sufficient, but that is not for the attainment of perfection.
O venerable one, how can knowledge devoid of yoga grant liberation in this world?
And yoga devoid of knowledge is likewise incapable of the task of liberation. (13)

Therefore, one who desires liberation should practice both knowledge and yoga with firm resolve. Since, as has been shown here, misfortune arises from attachment to the fluctuations of desire and the like, [the author asks]: "What is the means for attaining the state of the three-footed Bhūti (the Supreme Being) from this ghost of delusion? To this, he observes: [The following verse: "One should see here also... [is the response].
"Existence alone is real; everything else is unreal. There is nothing whatsoever apart from Brahman;

there is only Brahman, for the unreal does not exist"—from such scriptural statements, there arises the knowledge that negates the unreal phenomenal world as distinct from oneself, through which [the Self] is realized.

There is no dispute that there may be *vikalebara-kaivalya* (liberation with the physical body), characterized by abiding in the measure of the Brahman consisting of the three steps (*traipada-brahma-mātrā*), because one's status as a *jīva*— which arises from one's own ignorance— is terminated by one's own knowledge,
and such knowledge takes its locus in the final birth; for without that [final birth], there can be no knowledge of the appearance of the qualified [Brahman].

Because the cognition that appears as dependent on the mind of one bound by a deficiency in the aforementioned means is incapable of accomplishing its own fruit, and because even the yoga of appearances— which brings about various trivial accomplishments—
is incapable of attaining the fruit of primary yoga, such are these two: the cognition of appearances and yoga.
Since the two [means] are individually incapable of accomplishing their own respective fruits,

therefore one who desires liberation should practice knowledge (*jñāna*) and yoga (*yoga*) in combination. By that, the appearances of knowledge and yoga, having abandoned their own inherent appearance, [attain their true nature].

They culminate in the knowledge of Brahman alone, which is without counterpart and devoid of distinctions. Accordingly, the Śruti says: "For weapon is quenched by weapon; impurity is washed away by impurity," and so forth.
In that regard, the semblance of yoga (yogābhāsa), however, eliminates the semblance-status inherent in the knowledge of semblances.
He comes to rest in non-differentiated knowledge.
That fruit is of the nature of knowledge;
therefore, at the outset, it should be known that the object of knowledge is itself of the nature of knowledge, having knowledge alone as its means.
The seeker of liberation should investigate what ignorance is like, by knowing which one's own true nature—the state of absolute isolation (kaivalya), the supreme goal—is realized. (15)
This soul is liberated from defects such as desire, anger, and fear;
yet how is it that the living being, though enveloped by all defects, is released through knowledge? (16)
Just as knowledge, which is one's own essential nature, is full and all-pervading,
so too there is no difference between [that nature] and the defects such as desire and anger.
Afterwards, what indeed would be his injunction, and how could there even be a prohibition for him? The man of discrimination is forever liberated, free from the delusion of saṃsāra. || 18 ||
O Lotus-born One, that Truth is of a perfectly complete nature;
it is both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala), for it is indeed such because of its perfection.

Since this is so, keeping in mind that non-dual knowledge (*nirviśeṣa-jñāna*) must indeed be capable of accomplishing its own fruit, [the author] states "knowledge... (verse 14) to show that those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) must understand the extent of knowledge and ignorance.
Therein, he describes the nature of non-dual knowledge: "That which is known... and so forth. That very [knowledge]...
The meaning is "the knowledge as previously described. (p.
395) The meaning is that he who is such a knower becomes one who has accomplished his purpose (*kṛtakṛtya*).
Again, with the intention of referring to the knowledge of appearances (*ābhāsajñāna*), he raises an objection: "What [is it]?"?

"By all defects such as desire, anger, and so forth. Desires, anger, and the like are the manifestations of one's own ignorance (16). By demonstrating that [such defects] are impossible within one's own Self—which is established solely as the knowledge of itself that devours all defects—he sets them aside with the word "svātma" (one's own Self). As follows:

One's own nature is entirely complete; although it pervades all that exists as the pervasive [ground], it does not become differentiated because the knowledge regarding its objects culminates in that [nature] alone. One might object: "Even if there is no knowledge apart from one's own nature, defects such as desire and the like would still be distinct from it. To this, he says: "Desire... and so forth.

Indeed, how could there be any doubt—whether the multitude of defects such as desire exists or not—in the case of the non-dual Brahman alone? Nor can such a doubt be established by scripture (*smṛti*), because the state of being non-dual Brahman alone cannot tolerate even the scent of "this exists" or "that does not exist" apart from itself. Thus, the knower has accomplished all that was to be done.
He says "he becomes" and explains: "the one who is discerning" (vivekī). He states that this very person possesses the nature of Brahman: "the completely full" (paripūrṇa).

Since the knower of Brahman is free from the delusions of transmigratory existence, he is indeed Brahman; therefore, he says "the whole" (sakala), explaining that what is known as "Truth" (satya) assumes the state of being the "all" and so forth through the perspective of one's own ignorance and other such views. || 19 ||
There is no distinction between one who knows the manifestation and one who does not;
by means of *kalā*, which is the nature of creative manifestation, it has entered into the delusion of saṃsāra.
It is partless (*niṣkala*), stainless, directly manifest as the whole (*sakala*), and like the sky. (20)
How could he, having attained this form which is devoid of the knowledge of arising, persistence, dissolution, and manifestation, fall into the ocean of delusion? (21)
O mighty-armed one, having repeatedly abandoned knowledge, he sinks again and again into the delusions of pleasure, pain, and so forth, just as is the condition of those in saṃsāra. (22)
Likewise, when a man of knowledge remains permeated by latent impressions (vāsanā), there is no distinction between the two here; their perception of worldly existence is the same.
If knowledge is known to be of such a nature, then what, moreover, is ignorance?
[The text] says that one seems to partake in the state of transmigratory existence due to the conjunction with an internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that is non-luminous;
this form is characterized by such qualifiers as "that which is partless" (*niṣkala*), and so forth.

The Lord provides the answer to the question: "Even if one lacks the fourfold means for the purification of the mind (*cittaśuddhi*), if a knower (*jñānī*) has arrived by whatever means possible, he would then have accomplished his purpose; how could he, having abandoned his own innate knowledge, sink into the ocean of delusion like those who lack self-knowledge? He says: "Happily... (sukheti).
21–22 || Likewise, this one who possesses knowledge of appearances is also equal [to the former] through his own ignorance. 23 ||
This refers to the knowledge of one who possesses the knowledge of manifestation (*ābhāsajñānin*).
The meaning is that because there is no contradiction between the knowledge and ignorance of manifestation, it is logical for them to culminate in a single object.
For one who possesses the knowledge of manifestation, liberation is not accomplished without yoga.
One who is established in knowledge, though not dispassionate, knows the Dharma even while his senses remain unsubdued. || 24 ||
O Creator, even while in the body, one does not attain liberation without yoga.
Embodied beings are known to be of two kinds: the unripe and the fully ripened. (25)
Embodied beings who are unripe are devoid of yoga, whereas those who are ripe through yoga [attain the goal];
for by the fire of yoga, every body indeed becomes non-inert and free from sorrow.
But the earthen [element] should be known as inert; indeed, when unrefined, it causes suffering.

Regarding its lack of efficacy without yoga, he says: "By knowledge," etc. One who is established in knowledge superimposed upon it, who knows dharma from the scriptures, yet has not himself conquered his senses. || 24 ||

This knower of the appearance of consciousness, having merely washed away the impurity of the appearance residing within his own innate knowledge through yoga-less means and thereby attained pure knowledge, never attains liberation at that same time,
because the water of yoga alone purifies the impurities of the mind; for knowledge acquired by one whose mind is unpurified does not lead to it.

The meaning is that it becomes effective in producing its result. He states that there are two types of knowers, distinguished by the difference between the apparent (ābhāsa) and the ultimate (pāramārthika): "the unripe," etc. (verse 25). Those who possess knowledge of the mere appearance are "unripe" because their inner nature is impure. Those who are "ripe" through yoga are the knowers of the ultimate reality; this is the meaning.
He states the insentience and sentience of the body and so forth presided over by those possessing pure and impure knowledge, beginning with the word "sarva" (all).

It is appropriate that the body and other [limbs] of the knower are sentient because their impurities have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge; in this regard, there is the scriptural authority: "Just as a pot is made of clay, even so the body is composed of consciousness. || 26 ||
For those who possess knowledge of appearances, suffering is not ceased;
even while established in meditation, such a person remains thus powerless over the senses. (27)
Even though these [senses] are firmly restrained, one is nevertheless afflicted by others—by cold, heat, pleasure, pain, and the like, as well as by mental diseases. (28)
The body is afflicted by various other living beings, as well as by treatises, fire, water, and wind; consequently, the mind becomes agitated. (29)
Likewise, when there is a failure of the vital breaths, the wind becomes agitated;
consequently, the minds of men become disturbed and pervaded by hundreds of sufferings. (30)
At the time of the body's end, whatever one contemplates in the mind, that very thing becomes the living being; such is the cause of rebirth. (31)
Human beings do not know what birth will occur at the end of the body;
therefore, both knowledge and detachment are merely the exertion of the individual soul.
Just as an ant that has stung the body is released through meditation, how could it have been bitten by scorpions, or how could it be happy at the end of its bodily existence? (33)
Therefore, those who are enveloped by false reasoning do not understand this;

for even if one who possesses knowledge of appearances remains established in meditation like one of pure knowledge, he would become helpless because his collection of organs is not concentrated, thinking that there is nothing other than Brahman and that the senses and so forth do not exist. || 27 ||
These [rites] are to be performed according to one's capacity, for men who possess knowledge of Brahman without distinction from others.

30–31 || Since those who possess knowledge of appearances do not know [the truth] in this way, it is called "knowledge of appearances. If it is argued that even those who possess knowledge of the undifferentiated (nirviśeṣa) do not know [it] in this way, [the reply is: it is true; for if they perceive a body as distinct from Brahman, or a time of its dissolution, they would indeed know [it], because their realization is solely of the undifferentiated Brahman.

Because it is preceded by the negation of the delusion as to whether the collection of the state of ignorance and its effects— characterized by the body and so forth— exists or does not exist, it should be understood that the subject here is the one who possesses knowledge of the appearance (*ābhāsajñānī*). By the terms "knower" (*jñānin*) and "yogi," the primary knower and yogi are intended.

If it is argued that [the conduct] would be in accordance with the fundamental scripture (mūla-śruti) were they accepted, we say no; for even the fundamental scripture has as its purport subjects such as those who possess illusory knowledge (ābhāsa-jñānin), and because the conduct of the pure knower (śuddha-jñānin) has been clearly established in the fourth chapter. Indeed, never...

The meaning is that since the Śruti speaks of contradictory matters, it is appropriate to say that the Śruti describes the one who possesses illusory knowledge and the one who possesses ultimate knowledge as being distinct from one another. (32) It was stated that the knower of the illusory [self] must be specifically characterized in this section; therefore, he alone is characterized as follows: "the ant... (33).
Since there is thus the delusion that meditation on one's own body and its oppositions exist as something exceeding Brahman,
therefore—
The sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) alone is the root of all misfortune; indeed, for one in whom egoism (ahaṃkṛti) has perished, [all suffering ceases]. 34.
Even his body will not perish, let alone his diseases;
for whom will there be affliction from water, fire, weapons, pits, and the like? (35)
Whenever the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) becomes either utterly diminished or excessively nourished,
by that very means his [afflictions] perish, and diseases and the like arise.
An effect never exists without a cause;
likewise, how could suffering arise in the body without the ego-sense? (37)

Egoity [arises] toward the body and so forth imagined by one’s own ignorance. (34) Although, from the perspective of the ignorant, there may be a body—such as being cut by weapons or falling into a pit—for the knower, because he is bodiless (*videha*), there is no injury whatsoever for that very knower; this is the meaning. (35) If, however, the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*) should arise in him regarding the body and so forth, then...

He says that all misfortune arises for one who possesses their own ignorance (svājña), beginning with the words "When...": By this defect of identifying with the body, his mental modifications such as "I am Brahman" perish and become concealed. Furthermore, diseases and other afflictions manifest toward that person who identifies with the body. [Verse 36] It is indeed the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) itself...
He says that it is the root of all misfortune: "by reason of" (kāraṇena). || 37 ||
(399) The state of lordship and liberation while living (jīvanmuktatva) belongs to one perfected in yoga.
All things have been conquered by the body, yet the body itself has been conquered by the yogis;
how then can it produce for them results such as pleasure and pain? (38)
He by whom the senses, the mind, the intellect, and desire, anger, and the like have been conquered, has thereby conquered everything; he is not oppressed by anything whatsoever. (39)
The great elements and the principles are withdrawn in due order;
the body, composed of the seven constituents, is gradually consumed by the fire of yoga. (40)
Even by the gods, the body of the yogi of great power cannot be perceived;
he is liberated from the bonds of duality, the supreme bearer of manifold powers.
As is space, so is the body; yet it is even purer than space.
It is more subtle than the subtle, visible, both gross and non-gross, and both inert and conscious. 42.
For the lord of yogis, being independent, ageless, and immortal, can assume any form at will and sports playfully anywhere throughout the three worlds. (43)
The yogin, possessing inconceivable power and having conquered his senses, may assume various forms and withdraw them again at his own will. (44)
He does not undergo death, but rather [attains it] again through the power of yoga;
by means of haṭha he is as if dead, for how can there be death for one who is already dead? (45)
Where death prevails for all, there he truly lives;
where fools indeed live, there he is truly dead.
There is nothing at all that remains to be done for him; he is not tainted by what has been done. He is liberated while living, ever pure, and free from all defects. (47)

All are their own commands, by those yogis who have realized the identity of Brahman and the Self. (38) With the sword of knowledge that "nothing exists apart from Brahman," [they sever] the senses. (39) Furthermore—[they sever] the great elements.
(40) For the possessor of perfect knowledge, through the attainment of the state of the Lord, [powers such as] the fulfillment of true resolve [arise]. If...

When this body of one engaged in the yoga of right knowledge becomes invisible to all, and he strives for powers such as those of Īśvara and so forth, then [he is sought] even by the gods. (41–44) He does not undergo death, because death and the like reside in the body, and the yogin has transcended the body. Not.

According to the Vedic revelation, "The wise one is neither born nor dies," the very realization that there is no body or such thing apart from Brahman is indeed *haṭha*; by this *haṭha*, which is perfect knowledge, that body is truly dead. || 45 ||
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) beginning with "That which is night for all beings," and so forth. || 46-47 ||
The mockery of those who possess mere intellectual illumination is evident;
other wise men, though detached, are always conquered by their bodies.
How can those wretched embodied beings, who are but lumps of flesh, be equal to yogis? (48)
At the end of the body, the wise obtain the fruit of their merit and their sin;
having experienced such various results, the wise one shall become [liberated] once again. (49)

Having praised the one who possesses non-dual knowledge—whose mental impurities have been dispelled through yoga—as both the Lord and one liberated while living, he now ridicules those of "semblance-knowledge" (ābhāsajñānin) in comparison to him:
"Those who are detached," etc. Those who are intensely attached to objects other than themselves are [here called] "detached" (viraktāḥ). || 48 ||

Having experienced the fruits of karma such as *prārabdha*, the knower may be born again. For one who possesses ultimate knowledge (*pāramārthika-jñānin*), there is no merit or demerit, nor the resulting cycle of high and low births;
however, for one who possesses only apparent knowledge (*ābhāsa-jñānin*), all of this is possible—such is the intention of the Śruti. Otherwise, [if it were not so], one would know Brahman...

"He becomes Brahman indeed who knows it thus as seedless; he becomes truly seedless. Only the knower of that [Brahman] becomes immortal here; no other path for reaching [the goal] exists," and so forth.

The statement regarding non-rebirth, which restates the disembodied liberation (videhakaivalya) characterized by abiding solely as Brahman at the very moment of sensation, pertains to one who possesses knowledge that is merely apparent. || 49 ||
Through association with those perfected ones (siddhas), one subsequently attains the fulfillment of all goals by means of merit; one obtains association with a perfected being,
and through the grace of that perfected being, one becomes a yogi— otherwise it is not so.
"Then cyclic existence perishes; it is not otherwise, as Śiva has declared.

For one who possesses knowledge of such an appearance, through the excellence of their merit and by association with those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), the state of having accomplished all that was to be done (kṛtakṛtyatā) shall arise"—thus he says: "Afterwards," etc. (verse 50).
Knowledge and yoga stand in a mutual relationship of cause and effect;
O Creator, knowledge devoid of yoga does not lead to liberation. (51)
Without knowledge alone, yoga is never accomplished.
With the intention of referring to the combination of both appearance-knowledge and yoga, the disparagement of each one individually is stated by the words "by yoga" [and so forth]. || 51 ||
Yoga alone is the supreme path to liberation; and yoga is attained through knowledge over the course of many successive births. || 52 ||
But knowledge is produced through yoga alone in a single birth;
therefore, there is no path superior to yoga that bestows liberation.
Having investigated knowledge for a long time, one thinks, "I am liberated. Does he become liberated at that very moment simply by such reflection? (54)
Later, after hundreds of other births, one is liberated through yoga alone;
but for you, birth and death do not recur again and again because of yoga.
Through the union of prāṇa and apāna, the oneness of the moon and sun occurs;
by means of the fire, one will certainly color the body composed of the seven constituents.
His diseases perish; what need is there to mention [the cessation of] cutting, digging, and the like?
Thus, this embodied being remains in the form of the supreme ether.
But what is the use of saying more? Indeed, there is no death for him; he appears in the world like a person with a body, yet he is himself like burnt camphor.
He states the mutual relationship of cause and effect between the two: "Birth," etc. (52). Because it is thus, therefore [it is so]:

for, having swallowed the appearance residing within the cognition of appearance, it generates pure cognition. For this very reason, the path of yoga bestows liberation through the gateway of knowledge. (53)
In the absence of yoga, even by means of a semblance of knowledge, one should investigate through occasional reflection alone. || 54 ||

He praises yoga with the words, "one is liberated through yoga alone," meaning that birth and death do not occur for those who possess knowledge of the manifestation [of reality] as they do for others. (55) The body consists of the seven constituents (*dhātu*); since the body is composed of the seven constituents—white matter (*śukla*) and so forth—it is called "that" (*tam*), being identical with them. (56–58)

The arising of self-knowledge occurs only when the mind has been refined by yoga. In all living beings, the mind is bound to the vital breath (prāṇa), just as a bird is firmly tied with a rope; such is this mind. (59)
(403) However, by means of various types of mental inquiry, the mind does not become subdued;
therefore, the means for its conquest is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa), and not otherwise. (60)

O Creator, the vital breath (prāṇa) does not come under control through arguments, disputations, networks of scriptures, logical reasonings, mantras, or medicines, except by means of the perfected method (siddhopāya).
Without understanding that skillful means, one proceeds upon the path of yoga;
through fragmentary knowledge, one suddenly becomes even more afflicted by defilements. (62)
That yogi who, out of delusion, desires the yoga of the breaths without first conquering the vital air, is like one who wishes to cross the ocean while mounted upon an unbaked clay pot.
If the vital breath has dissolved within while the practitioner is still alive and his body has not yet fallen, his mind is tormented by defects.

The meaning is that it makes its own self, which is established [within], an object of cognition. This mind is like that, for the scripture states: "O dear one, the mind is indeed bound by the vital breath" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.2). Since this is so, therefore...
The very first task is the practice of yoga;
when the mind is purified, the knowledge of one's own self shines forth.
Therefore, O Lotus-born One, through yoga, knowledge shall arise in a single lifetime.
Therefore, the practitioner should constantly practice that very yoga at the outset;
those seeking liberation must achieve mastery over the vital breath for the sake of liberation.
There is no merit higher than yoga; there is no auspiciousness higher than yoga; there is nothing subtler than yoga; indeed, there is nothing higher than yoga. (67)

That which is the unification of the apāna and prāṇa breaths, as well as of the rajas and the semen, the conjunction of the sun and the moon, and of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman). (68)
Thus, the conjunction of the net of dualities is called yoga;
since yoga possesses such power, therefore— [66–68]
The Instruction on the Pinnacle of Yoga: Now I shall proclaim the Pinnacle of Yoga, which is the most excellent among all forms of knowledge. (69)
When one meditates upon the mantra, a trembling of the limbs arises;
having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) or whichever other posture is pleasing.
Fixing one's gaze on the tip of the nose, with hands and feet restrained, and withdrawing the mind from everything else, one should contemplate the syllable Oṃ there.
The wise one constantly meditates, having placed the Supreme Lord within the heart—
that [body] which has a single pillar, nine gates, three posts, and five deities.
But within such a body, a wise person should not perceive [the self] as having the form of the solar disc, filled with the blazing of rays. (73)
The fire situated within that [central channel] blazes like the wick of a lamp;
that measure which is the flame of the lamp is the measure of the Supreme Lord.

(p. 405) Having thus praised Yoga, he now elaborates upon the *śikhā* (crest), which is the very essence of Yoga—beginning with the word "atha" (now). It is called the *yogaśikhā* because it shines forth at the pinnacle of Yoga. It is [so called] because it swallows the appearances (*ābhāsa*) residing in the knowledge that takes impure mind as its support. That [Yogaśikhā], I shall declare to you.
This is the meaning. [Verse 69] To the question "What is that?", he states its extent and the sequence of its practice, beginning with the words "When":

*mantra* is the resonance (*nāda*) because it protects (*trāyate*) the thinker (*mantṛ*), the one who reflects. When the *mantra*—that is, the resonance—is meditated upon, that is, when it is reflected upon, then immediately thereafter, the trembling of the limbs of the yogi occurs.
It arises; for the purpose of pacifying that, there is the "posture" (āsana), as well as whatever else is pleasing, such as Siddhāsana and so forth.

70. Thus, having remained on the seat, [one should focus] at the tip of the nose; 71. at that time, one should not direct the gaze toward the body. He says this with the word "eka" (single): because the body is the support for the pavilion of the spinal column (*vīṇā-daṇḍa*), the word "pillar" (*sthūṇa*) refers to the three types of karma, such as those yet to come (*āgāmi*). By the word "five deities" (*pañca-daivata*)...

The five Brahmās, beginning with Brahmā and ending with Sadāśiva, are thus described. The meaning is that one should not maintain the perception of "self" and "belonging to the self" toward this aggregate body. To the question of what should be done after that, [the answer is] "in one's own heart, [meditating on] the Sun," by means of meditation conducive to *prāṇāyāma*.

The meaning is that one should meditate upon [the Supreme Lord] as being joined with a series of flames of fire located in the *mūlādhāra*. Regarding this, he says "dīpaśikhā" (lamp-flame), stating that the Supreme Lord is to be meditated upon there in the form of a lamp-flame.
As for the lamp-flame situated in the *mūlādhāra*, that measure which is even thinner than the awn of a grain of *nīvāra*—that is the measure.
When the Supreme Lord has been meditated upon in that form, || 74 ||
Through the practice of yoga, there is the direct realization of the supreme state.
Indeed, by the practice of yoga, yogis pierce the sun and reach the second gate, the perfectly pure Suṣumnā. 75.
Having drunk from the hollowed cup of the skull, one then beholds that state.

Furthermore, by the grace of that [state] and through the power of yoga practice, yogins pierce the solar orb and proceed to that state; for it is stated in the Śruti: "Through the gate of the sun, they, free from passion, depart."
Seeing a man who has renounced the world, the sun moves from its place, thinking:
"Having pierced through my orb, he shall go to the Supreme Brahman."

Thus, in accordance with the *Smṛti*, it has been stated that the practitioners of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-yogins*) pierce the solar orb and proceed to that state. But as for the practitioners of yoga alone (*kevala-yogins*), having pierced the second door, the *suṣumnā*, by means of the *kuṇḍalinī*, they [ascend] through that path to the thousand-petaled wheel (*sahasrāra-cakra*), which is enclosed within the digits of time (*kalā*). || 75 ||

Having entered there and drunk the nectar born of the sun, moon, and fire, he—or they—perceives that state, whether it be the fourth (*turya*) or that which transcends the fourth (*turyātīta*), as "I am That. Thereupon, in accordance with the knowledge acquired therein, they proceed toward Brahman, whether with attributes (*saviśeṣa*) or without attributes (*nirviśeṣa*); this is the meaning.
For one incapable of meditative absorption, there is the attainment of a meritorious world; yet, if that being meditates upon it due to indolence and negligence, [the result is otherwise]. (76)
If one should come at the three times of day, he shall attain the perfection of merit;
having attained this merit, I have described it to you in brief.

He speaks of the attainment of meritorious worlds for those unable to meditate in this manner: "Now," etc. If a living being, due to laziness or negligence, meditates upon—that is, contemplates—that Brahman with a sense of duality because it is not properly integrated into the process of meditation; [76] if such a person should thus engage in meditation three times every day.

This sage performs meditation; by virtue of his own contemplation, he would attain—that is, reach—the perfection of merit and the sovereignty of Brahmā, Indra, and others. The meaning is that this has been stated by me in brief according to the influence of such merit. || 77 ||
For one who has attained yoga, there is the awakening to one's own self;
then, having attained yoga, he perceives the serene Supreme Lord when, indeed, his defilement has been exhausted over thousands of previous births. (78)
Then, through yoga, he perceives the great destruction of saṃsāra.
Having attained yoga in the manner to be described, he realizes his own Self; thus [the author] says:
"Having attained... He should realize, "I am that. [This applies] to those who are burdened by sin.
To the question, "From where does the direct realization of the Lord arise for the purpose of cutting off the conception of anything other than oneself? he says:
"janmāntara... etc. [It arises] when, through the grace of the Lord—who is satisfied by the offering of the fruits of obligatory and other rites—[realization occurs].
(p. 407) Now I shall fully explain the approach to the Guru after having mastered the vital breaths for the sake of practicing yoga, as well as the characteristics of the practice of yoga. (79)
One should always serve that Guru by whom mastery over the winds (marujjaya) has been accomplished;
through the grace of the Guru’s mouth, the wise man should achieve mastery over the vital breaths (prāṇajaya). 80.

It was stated that "then one sees through yoga"; in response to the inquiry as to what kind of yoga this is, [the author] now describes its extent, along with its means and its fruit, beginning with the word "adhunā" (now).
79 || He states that this must be known solely from the mouth of the Guru: "The wind," etc. 80 ||
The movement of the Sarasvatī is said to be one vitasti in length and four aṅgulas in width;
it is soft and white, and such are the characteristics of the garment for wrapping.
First, preceded by the movement of the Sarasvatī channel, he describes the state of Kuṇḍalinī and the means for its movement, beginning with the word "vitasti":
having wrapped the head of the Sarasvatī channel with a cloth characterized by the previously mentioned definition, during the Brāhma-muhūrta...
Having risen, for a period of one muhūrta, he should move it fearlessly. || 81 ||

By the movement of Kuṇḍalī, the three knots are pierced; having firmly restrained the vital air through the technique of activating the Śakti, one should straighten the Kuṇḍalī which was coiled eightfold. (82)
One should perform the contraction of the anus and then stir the Kuṇḍalinī;
for such a person, even if he has entered the mouth of death, whence can there be fear of death? (83)
This very supreme secret has been told by me to you:
seated upon the vajra-posture, one should constantly practice the upward contraction. (84)
The fire, kindled by the vital wind (vāyu), should incessantly burn the Kuṇḍalinī;
heated by that fire, the life-force (jīvā-śakti) becomes the enchantress of the three worlds. (85)
When it enters the interior of the mouth of the Suṣumṇā during the lunar staff (candradaṇḍa),
it pierces the Brahma-knot together with the wind and the fire.
Then, having pierced the Viṣṇu-knot, one remains at the Rudra-knot;
thereafter, one should fill [the body] intensely with kumbhakas again and again.
Having restrained [the breath] after the movement of the Sarasvatī channel, then at the anus;
he states that through the movement of Kuṇḍalinī, this [practitioner] attains freedom from death, saying: "from the mouth of Death" (mṛtyuvaktrāt). || 82–83 ||
Regarding what was stated—that one should move the *kuṇḍalinī*—he explains that along with its method: "By the thunderbolt," etc. (84).

By the wind arising from contraction; by that burning, she is tormented. (85) Then, as to what she does, it says "she enters. Because the Suṣumnā is cool like the moon, its capacity to pacify the heat of Kuṇḍalinī is established through the experience of yoga; this is the meaning. By the gaze and the vital breath.
The Brahma-granthi, which resembles a door-bolt on the path for entering the mūlādhāra.
The unstruck door is the Viṣṇu-knot. It is located at the door of the Ājñā [cakra], which is the Rudra-knot.
He states the means for piercing the Rudra-knot with the word "tataḥ" (then). || 87 ||
The procedure for the fourfold kumbhaka: Now one should practice Sūryabheda, Ujjāyī, and Śītalī, as well as Bhastrā; together, these constitute the fourfold kumbhaka. (88)
Endowed with the three bandhas, it brings about the attainment of the absolute (kevala). He describes the varieties of kumbhaka with the words "Now" (atha) etc. (verses 88–89).
(p. 409) Now, I shall correctly explain in brief the characteristics of the *sūryakumbhaka* and its [related] characteristics. || 89 ||
Having approached a secluded place alone,
one who eats light food and possesses fortitude should meditate upon the supreme reality, the immortal essence consisting of *prāṇa* and the rest.
It is the peerless medicine that removes the disease of saṃsāra. || 90 ||
Having drawn in the breath through the solar channel (sūryanāḍī) by means of the yoga of practice,
and having performed the retention (kumbhaka) according to the rules, the practitioner should exhale through the cool-rayed [channel] (candrānāḍī).
It destroys many diseases of the stomach and eliminates the affliction of worms;
this should be performed repeatedly and is declared as Sūryabheda. 92.
First, the characteristic of the collective [practice] is stated: "Alone... (90). Then, he states the characteristic of the *sūryabheda* [breathing technique] and its fruit: "The sun... (91–92).
The characteristic of Ujjāyī Kumbhaka:
Having drawn in the breath through both nostrils, one should cast it into the sides of the Kuṇḍalinī; thereafter, the wise practitioner should retain it in the abdomen and exhale through the Iḍā. 93.

It destroys the defects such as phlegm in the throat, increases the digestive fire of the body, removes water from the channels, and eliminates the defects residing in the bodily constituents (dhātus). || 94 ||
Whether walking or standing, one should perform the *kumbhaka* known as *ujjāyī*.
He states the definition of the *ujjāyī-kumbhaka*: "Through the two channels... (verses 93–94).
The characteristic of the *śītalī* kumbhaka is as follows: having drawn in the air through the mouth, one should exhale it through the nostrils. (95)
And this Śītalī-karaṇa destroys bile, hunger, and thirst.
He states the definition of Śītalī as follows: "with the mouth," etc. (95).
Now, the characteristic of the bellows-retention (*bhastrikā-kumbhaka*):
like a blacksmith's bellows, [the breath] moves rapidly between the two breasts. (96)
One should mentally fill the air residing within the body until it reaches the āśrama;
one should fill it with the breath of the sun (sūrya) in such a way that exertion arises in the body. 97.
Having performed the contraction of the throat, one should exhale again through the moon (the left nostril);
this removes wind, bile, and phlegm, and increases the digestive fire of the body. (98)
It awakens the Kuṇḍalinī, destroys defects of the mouth, bestows auspiciousness and happiness, and removes the obstructions such as phlegm situated within the opening of the Brahma-nāḍī. (99)
This kumbhaka known as bhastrā must indeed be performed specifically; it arises from the correct binding and effects the piercing of the three knots. 100.
He states the characteristics of the *bhastrikā* and *kumbhaka* breath-retentions with the words "of the breasts," etc.

[Verse 96–99]: "Then, simultaneously with the movement of the bellows-like breasts... [Verse 100]: The meaning is that even the *rudragranthi* (the knot of Rudra) is pierced by means of the *bhastrikā-kumbhaka*.
The Procedure for the Three Bandhas:
Now I shall describe the three bandhas in their proper order;
by performing them regularly, one attains mastery over the vital breath (vāyu). (101)
When the fourfold division of *kumbhaka* has been established, these three *bandhas* must be performed; for that shall indeed be described by me. (102)
The first is the root-lock (mūlabandha), the second is named the upward-flying lock (uḍḍīyanabandha), and the third is the throat-lock (jālandharabandha); I shall now describe their characteristics.
He states the definition of the three *bandhas* as being ancillary to the fourfold *kumbhaka*: "The *bandhas*... and so forth.
The root-lock (mūlabandha):
having firmly pressed the anus with the heel, one should forcefully contract the vital air so that the wind repeatedly moves upward. (104)
The prāṇa and apāna, as well as the nāda and bindu, attain oneness through the mūlabandha;
they bestow the perfect accomplishment of yoga—of this there is no doubt. || 105 ||
By the terms *nāda* and *bindu*, the intellect (*buddhi*) and the mind (*manas*) are expressed. || 105–107 ||

The Uḍḍiyāṇa-bandha should be performed at the end of the kumbhaka and at the beginning of the recaka; it is called Uḍḍiyāṇa because by means of this bandha, the vital breath (prāṇa) is made to fly up into the Suṣumnā. (106)
Therefore, this is proclaimed by yogis as Uḍḍīyaṇa;
indeed, Uḍḍīyaṇa is always said by the Guru to be innate (sahaja). 107.
One should practice this without weariness; even an old man will become young again.
One should diligently perform the contraction both above and below the navel. (108)
If one practices this for six months, one certainly conquers death; there is no doubt.
(108–111) *Tāṇa* means contraction.
The Jālandhara-bandha should be performed at the end of the inhalation (pūraka); it is the bandha known by the name Jālandhara. || 109 ||
This [bandha], consisting of the contraction of the throat, obstructs the path of the vital air;
contracting the throat, one should firmly fix it in the heart by means of willpower. || 110 ||
This is the bindu known as Jālandhara, which effects the nourishment of nectar;
when the constriction of the throat is quickly performed by contracting [the muscles] below. || 111 ||
In the center, by means of the western contraction, the vital breath (prāṇa) enters the Brahma-nāḍī;
through the piercing of the three knots of Kuṇḍalinī, the attainment of the non-conceptual state occurs.
The yogi, seated in the vajra posture, having stirred Kuṇḍalinī... (112)
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the bellows-breathing (bhastrī) and quickly awaken Kuṇḍalinī;
the knots in the channel (vaṃśa) are then pierced by means of a heated iron rod.
In the same way, there may be a splitting of a knot in the spinal column due to the wind;
when an ant is clinging there, itching arises in that spot. (114)
Likewise, through constant practice upon the Suṣumnā with the vital breath (vāyu), one then pierces the Rudra-knot and proceeds to that which is of the nature of Śiva. || 115 ||
Having made the moon and the sun equal, their union proceeds;
by piercing the three knots, one transcends the three qualities (guṇas).
In the union of Śiva and Śakti, the supreme state arises;
the yogi, liberated from the three bonds, [attains] the Vajrāsana. (112–116)
Śiva is indeed the Fourth State (turiya) situated at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), while Śakti is Kuṇḍalinī;
the meaning is that from the union of these two alone arises the supreme state, the innate condition free from conceptual construction (sahaja-nirvikalpaka-avasthā).
The Suṣumnā is the path to liberation and the enjoyer of time;
just as an elephant always drinks water with its very trunk, [so does one drink through it]. 117.
One should likewise swallow the blowing wind through the vajra-stalk of the suṣumnā;
and the twenty-one jewels arise from the vajra-staff. (118)
All [the channels] reside within the Suṣumnā like clusters of jewels on a thread;
established upon the path to liberation, the Suṣumnā is the embodiment of the universe.
Just as time is determined by the movement of the moon and sun, so too, when the breath is filled and confined within the jar-like body, it does not go outside for the practitioner.
Again and again, in the same manner, the characteristic of the western gate is fulfilled;
having been filled by those gates, it attains a slight state of breath-retention (*kumbhaka*).
The wind should enter all the limbs by way of the western path;
when exhaled, it reaches a state of depletion, and when inhaled, it then provides nourishment.
Regarding the statement that one should drink the vital breath and water through the *suṣumṇā*, he provides an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as).
117. That which is called the Vajradaṇḍa is the neck of the lute resting upon the Suṣumnā;

the twenty-one jewels located there are like lumps of flesh resembling chickpeas, which, because they swallow the darkness situated within the path of the Suṣumnā, exist in the form of light like lamps.

The meaning is that [the centers] exist like the joints of the bamboo-stalk of the *suṣumnā*, extending from the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra*, and they become directly perceptible to yogis. He states that such a *suṣumnā* is the path to liberation and the enjoyer of time with the words "mokṣa... and so forth.
She possesses manifold forms because she rests upon Brahman, the support of the universe. || 119 ||
The meaning is that this Suṣumnā is the "consumer of time," wherein the duration from a single blink of an eye up to the end of a kalpa is dissolved.
When the practitioner-yogin fills and retains the breath within that Suṣumnā which resides in him,
it becomes the sustainer of the calculation of time— from a momentary blink to the end of a kalpa— in the form of inhalation and exhalation.

The vital breath (prāṇavāyu) does not suddenly go outside; therefore, the meaning is that the state of being the enjoyer of time is established for the Suṣumnā. (120) If, through negligence, it goes outside of the Suṣumnā, then again and again, just as before, one should fill the breath through the Suṣumnā and perform retention (kumbhaka).

That which constitutes the characteristic of the western gate is this very *prāṇa*; having been filled through those gates and that specific gate, it first assumes a slight state of *kumbhaka* (retention). Then, the *prāṇa-vāyu* should enter all the limbs via the western path, if...

Through the conjunction of time and action, the air exhaled via the *suṣumnā* reaches a state of depletion; thereafter, when it is filled [back in], it nourishes the body—that is to say, it brings about nourishment. || 122 ||
Through the yoga of the *suṣumnā*, the attainment of the knowledge of Brahman occurs; by means of that yoga, he causes the mind— which was born together with the entire body— to dissolve right there.
He alone is liberated, free from egoism, and happy;
for the fools who subsist on mere physical bodies do not understand this.
If the mind were destroyed when it has been spoken, then even the wind would be perceived as destroyed;
yet if it were not so, then there would be no scripture for it.
There is no realization of the self, no teacher, and no liberation. || 124 ||
Just as a jackal forcibly draws blood toward itself,
so too does the channel of Brahmā [draw] the bodily constituents through the power of continuous practice.
By this yoga of constant practice through the binding of the posture, the mind attains a state of dissolution, and the *bindu* does not descend below. (126)

He says "where" to show that only he who possesses the knowledge of the Self—which is the substratum for the superimposition and negation of the mind and its various effects as something separate from Himself—is truly liberated; such a one is freed from the delusion of anything other than Himself. Conversely, those who do not know the true nature of this substratum are the deluded.
The meaning is that because their vision is obscured by these three veils, their state of delusion is established. || 123 ||

He says "the mind" (cittam) to show that for one in whom such knowledge of the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna) does not arise, from their perspective, there is no such thing as the Vedas, the teacher, the knowledge arising therefrom, its fruit, liberation, and so forth;
the meaning is that their birth is in vain. For this reason: [he says] "this."

The absence of knowledge regarding the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the cause of misfortune; therefore, the subsequent text is commenced for the purpose of awakening that [knowledge]. While the constituent elements (*dhātu*) exist as distinct from Brahman, how can the knowledge of Brahman arise?
In this regard, the *jambūka* swallows the elements through the *suṣumnā* like blood; thereafter, the knowledge of Brahman is born.

Thus he says: "The jackal. In this manner, the Brahma-nāḍī indeed swallows the elements (dhātu) as well as external objects and their corresponding perceptions. Thereupon, the knowledge of Brahman arises, and simultaneously with that, there occurs liberation from the delusion of anything other than oneself. Such is the means for attaining perfection.
"Continuity" means that through yoga, the accomplishment of the stated purpose will occur. (125) Regarding what might result from practice, it is said: "by this. (126)
The sequence for achieving stability in one's true nature through the practice of yoga is as follows:
having abandoned both exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), one remains steady by means of the vital air;
various internal sounds arise, and the lunar orb flows forth.
Then, at that time, all defects such as hunger and thirst perish;
one attains a state of abiding solely in one's own nature, which is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
This characteristic of practice has indeed been told to you out of affection.
As for what would happen thereafter, it is this: when the breath becomes steady, then various sounds arise. Thus, through the tasting of the nectar, there is nothing beyond Brahman.
And through the awakening that "something exists," they perish, and so forth. || 128 ||
Mahāyoga consists of the fourfold yoga beginning with mantra:
mantra, laya, haṭha, and ending with rājayoga; these are the stages in successive order. (129)
This single Great Yoga is said to be fourfold. To explain that further, he says: "Mantra" [and so forth]. || 129 ||
In mantra-yoga,
[the breath] goes out with the syllable *ha* and enters again with the syllable *sa*.
This mantra "haṃsa, haṃsa" is recited by all living beings;
however, through the word of the Guru, the recitation becomes reversed within the suṣumnā.

"That which consists of the mantra-yoga [repeating] 'so'ham, so'ham' is what is called [mantra-yoga]. First, he states the definition of mantra-yoga with the words "by the letter *ha*" (verse 130). This mantra is always involuntarily recited by everyone in the form of inhalation and exhalation; it belongs only to those who are not yogis.
The meaning is that it occurs; however, for yogins, it arises from the words of the guru. || 131 ||
Haṭhayoga arises from the yoga of mantra and perception on the Western Path. || 132 ||
By the letter *ha* there is the sun, and by the letter *sa* the moon is said to be;
the unification of the sun and the moon is designated as *haṭha*. (133)

Desiring to explain later the yoga of rhythmic flow (*layayoga*) as recited in the scriptural sentences, he states the definition of *haṭhayoga*: "By the letter *ha*... (132). He says that the unification of the moon and the sun occurs: "By the letter *ha*... (133).

Laya-yoga is seized through Haṭha; [otherwise] there is dullness arising from all defects. When the identity of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and the supreme self (paramātman) occurs, [that is Laya-yoga]. || 134 ||
O Brahmin, when that unity is accomplished, the mind attains dissolution;
and when the arising of *laya-yoga* occurs, the vital breath attains steadiness. (135)
From absorption (laya), bliss is attained—the supreme state of the bliss of one's own Self.
He states the definition of the yoga of absorption (layayoga) with the words, "By force" (haṭhena). || 134-135 ||
The Rājayoga is in the great field in the center of the yoni, resembling the Japā flower or the Bandhūka flower.
The principle of Rajas dwells within living beings, completely enveloping the principle of the Goddess;
through the union of Rajas and Retas, it is known as Rājayoga. (137)
Having attained the state of *aṇimā* and the other [siddhis], one shines by means of *rājayoga*.
He states the definition of *rājayoga*: "From the union of the *yoni*, the *śakti*, and *Śiva*... (verse 137).
Thus, *rājayoga* arises from the conjunction of the *śakti* and *Śiva* within the *yoni*. (verse 137).
The essential nature of yoga in general, the attainment of liberation through yoga, the union of prāṇa and apāna, and the fourfold yoga are what should be known. || 138 ||
O Brahmin, this which was spoken by Śiva has been told in brief; it cannot be otherwise.
That which is to be attained is reached through gradual practice alone, and not otherwise.
Through the gradual practice of yoga with this very body, liberation is attained after a long time; that is indeed the "monkey's leap" method. (140)
He states that even the fourfold yoga, beginning with mantra, culminates in a single goal—namely, "prāṇa," etc.
The meaning is that within all four types of yoga, the union of prāṇa and apāna is the same. (138) Thus, he briefly states the fruit of the yoga taught by himself: "in sequence," etc.

The meaning is that, like liberation (kaivalya) which is attained simultaneously with the knowledge of the undifferentiated Brahman, the fruit of yoga is not intended to be attained immediately. || 139-140 ||
The manner in which one who has died without achieving perfection attains perfection in a future birth:
"If the body perishes through negligence before the perfection of yoga is attained, one endowed with the impressions of previous practice shall obtain another body. (141)
Then, by the power of merit, having attained perfection and being united with the Guru,
one quickly attains the fruit through the path of the western gate.

Due to practice performed in previous births, one attains the fruit quickly. [Objection: If the body of a practitioner of yoga perishes before the attainment of the fruit of yoga, then the labor he has exerted becomes fruitless; therefore, the Lord says: "The yogi... In that case, this yogi—
By means of former habitual tendencies. || 141–142 ||
Liberation arises solely from the yoga of practice;
this indeed is what must be understood—that is called the "crow's maxim" (kākamatam). || 143 ||
There is no doctrine superior to this one called "Practice" (Abhyāsa), which is other than the "Crow's Viewpoint" (Kākamatā).
By that alone is liberation attained, and not otherwise; so it was spoken by Śiva. 144.

(p. 419) He praises that very [state] with the words "this" (*etad*). By the word *kiṃ* (what), used in the sense of an objection—namely, "What is her actual state?"—*māyā* is expressed. He under whose control she remains is this crow, the Illusory One (*māyī*), the Great Lord (*maheśvara*). As it is said: "One should know *māyā* to be *prakṛti*, and the possessor of *māyā* (*māyin*)..."
"Maheśvara"—this very doctrine is known as the yoga of practice concerning Maheśvara, the "crow" established by the Śruti. 143.

The meaning is that because it serves as the cause for the knowledge of the non-dual Brahman by means of cleansing the impurity of the mind of both the ignorant and those with fallacious knowledge, liberation is generally attained through that alone in the Kali age, and not otherwise. || 144 ||

For the yogi, the attainment of all sovereign powers, liberation while living (jīvanmukti), and other such siddhis occurs through the sequence of Haṭhayoga; [otherwise] there would be no reaching the pinnacle, nor the dissolution of the vital breaths (prāṇas) along with the body, nor the path to liberation, without the well-known Western [tradition]. 145.
First, diseases perish, and afterwards, dullness born of the body [vanishes].
Then, having become the equalized essence (samarasa), the Moon rains down incessantly. (146)
Then the fire, together with the wind, gathers the elements;
various sounds arise, and the body becomes supple.
Having conquered dullness caused by rain and other such factors, that man becomes a sky-walker;
he becomes omniscient, able to assume any form at will, and possesses the speed of the wind. || 148 ||
He sports in the three worlds, and all supernatural powers (siddhis) arise;
when camphor dissolves, what hardness can remain there? || 149 ||
Likewise, when the ego-sense has perished, how could there be any hardness in the body?
And the lord of yogis is the creator of all, independent, and possessed of infinite forms. (150)
One becomes a great yogi liberated while living; there is no doubt about this. (p.

420) He praises Haṭhayoga, beginning with the word "Haṭha": "Uncreated and unartificial... ascending upwards through those two, one attains immortality; the Suṣumnā is indeed merged in the Supreme, free from passion, and of the nature of Brahman."

The meaning is this: that collection of objects well-known from such scriptural passages as these—wherein the dissolution and so forth of the various things occurs together with their respective cognitions for the living yogi—is accomplished through the practice of the sequence of Haṭhayoga; and apart from this final path of liberation, the "Great Path" (Mahāpatha), there exists no other ultimate goal for yogis whatsoever.

|| 145 || Preceded by a praise of such a yoga, he lauds the yogin— who is adorned with various kinds of supernatural powers— as one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and as a lord (īśvara), beginning with the words "In the beginning": "In the beginning," that is, even during the stage of practice, [he overcomes] all diseases, including physical ailments such as laziness and the like.

Through the union of the vital breath (prāṇa), fire, sun, moon, śakti, and Śiva, the moon incessantly and continuously rains down a stream of nectar. Then, the fire residing in the mūlādhāra, abiding together with the wind,
gathers the bodily constituents and brings about an increase in strength and the stabilization of virility.

The meaning is that he should act [thus]. "Mārdavam" means becoming as soft as a child; this is the sense. || 147 || Having conquered [the elements], having become like a cloud, and having abandoned such dullness as "becoming a cloud," that man becomes a sky-walker (khecara) through his splendor;
the meaning is that this yogi, through such practice, becomes the Sun. Furthermore—

The Omniscient One (sarvajña) [is such] because [all things] arise by His mere will. Furthermore, as to how His physical body abandons hardness and attains softness, he provides the answer with an illustration:
"camphor" (karpūra). Due to contact with the flame of a lamp, [hardness leaves] the camphor. Through the fire of yoga, when the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) is destroyed, [the body likewise becomes supple].
The meaning is that he may possess a body of softness or a body of space; furthermore, he is the creator of all.
The method for concealing artificial and non-artificial accomplishments:
"In this world, accomplishments are considered to be of two kinds, namely, the fabricated and the unfabricated. (151)

Those accomplishments which are achieved through means such as the application of medicinal elixirs, ritual procedures, networks of mantras, and repeated practice, are proclaimed to be "imagined" (kalpita). || 152 ||
Those accomplishments arising from ritual practice are impermanent and of little power;
indeed, they arise quite spontaneously even without such practice.

For those who are solely devoted to the yoga of their own Self, the many supernatural powers (siddhis) that arise through their sovereignty are known to be dear to the Lord and are considered free from conceptual construction.
Established, eternal, and of great power, these [attainments] take forms at will and are born of one's own yoga;
they arise after a long time even in those who are free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*). (155)
But those [powers] of the great yogi are always hidden within the imperishable state of the Supreme Self; their concealment without purpose is the characteristic of one perfected in yoga. || 156 ||
Regarding the question of how many kinds of yogic accomplishments (*siddhi*) there are, he states that they are of two types, distinguished as artificial and non-artificial:
"They are twofold" (verses 151–152). However, the non-artificial ones arise through practice (*sādhana*).
153–154 || These are accomplished by oneself alone. 155 || He states their need for concealment with the words "tāstu" (but those):

by a yogi established in the state of the Supreme Self through great yoga, these accomplishments (*siddhis*) must be concealed when not required for a specific purpose. That the entire web of accomplishments must always remain hidden and protected—this is what [is meant].
The meaning is that the characteristic of one who has attained perfection through that yoga is "innate" (sahaja). || 156 ||
This indicates the states of one perfected in yoga and one liberated while living:
"Just as various holy places and various paths are seen on the road by travelers proceeding toward the sky, so too are the various paths and the spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). (157)
They arise spontaneously in that which is devoid of gain and loss;
likewise, this web of accomplishments proceeds upon the path of yoga. 158.
Just as gold is thoroughly tested by expert goldsmiths, so too should one recognize the perfected one who is liberated while living. || 159 ||
His extraordinary qualities will certainly be seen at some point;
however, one should recognize a man who is devoid of supernatural powers as being bound. || 160 ||

(422) Since it might be thought that the *siddhis* would belong only to yogins as things intended by their own resolve, he says "just as" (*yathā*). With a specific result in view, likewise various paths of *siddhis* are seen for yogins even by chance. (157) [The *siddhis*] arise spontaneously in the yogin; just as there are sacred sites (*tīrthas*) on the path of the sky.

They are seen on the path of yoga. Just as a goldsmith examines gold, one should examine a perfected being (*siddha*) by means of his supernatural powers (*siddhis*). If those powers are present in him, then one should know that perfected being to be liberated; if they are not present, then one should know him to be bound. Thus he says: "by examiners."

If this person is a man of knowledge (jñānin), then he is one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). If [the state] exists in him, then—due to long-standing familiarity—it is extraordinary; [this refers] to that [state] in him.
Even while the body exists, the knower attains liberation without a body; for he alone is the one liberated while living, whose physical frame is ageless and immortal.
Indeed, cattle, chickens, insects, and the like meet with death. (161)
O Lotus-born One, how can there be liberation for them through alms-food?
Since the external breath does not enter, how can there be the falling of a body? (162)
The liberation that comes through alms-food is not destroyed;
when the state of Brahman has been attained within the body, it is like salt dissolving in water. (163)
When it attains non-difference [from the Self], then it is said to be liberated;
for the bodies and likewise the sense organs are considered distinct. || 164 ||
Brahman has attained the state of a body, just as water attains the state of bubbles.

If this one is a knower endowed with yoga, then [the text says] "ajarā" (undecaying). How can there be an undecaying and immortal physical body (*piṇḍa*) for the knower of yoga? If the physical body were indeed undecaying and immortal, then for him—
Since even a dream of liberation from the body characterized by alms-food is difficult to obtain, he says: "paśca" (afterwards).

161. The yogin’s external breath does not return. 162. Regarding the statement "liberation arises from the falling away of the body (piṇḍapāta)," the interrogative sense of "not" (*na*) implies that it is *not* the case that [liberation] is destroyed; rather, the meaning is that it is indeed destroyed. As for the question "How is liberation while in the body (videhamukti) [attained]?"—it is here said "the body": the effect of waters is salt (saindhava).

The meaning is that one becomes liberated while in the disembodied state (*videhamukta*) through the absence of the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding the appearance of the body and so forth, which is presented by the perceptions of others. This is because liberation while in the disembodied state is preceded by the negation of the delusion that anything exists or does not exist apart from oneself; thus, there is nothing apart from one's own self alone.
In that [Reality] wherein the perception of body, breath, auspiciousness, individual soul, the world, and the supreme self—
this manifold perception— does not truly shine forth.
I am that Rāmacandra, liberated while yet embodied.

Thus, from the statement of the Great Saying regarding disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*), the meaning is that the knower alone— due to the impossibility of any absolute identification with the body and so forth— is liberated while in the body even when viewed by others; otherwise, [one would think], "Now I have this body and so forth."
Through the conceit of "I" and "mine," the world appears as if real, and by that the living being (jīva) becomes bound; now, however,
the body and so forth are seen as false through both the empirical and the phenomenal perspectives—
whether one be liberated while living (jīvanmukta), or, after the fall of this present body, liberated without a body (videhamukta).

For those who possess the mental construction of something other than themselves—thinking "I shall become"—liberation from the body (videhamukti) ought to be impossible; indeed, even in their dreams, such liberation cannot possibly occur for them, because they continue to follow after the appearance of a body as something separate from themselves. This is the point.
At that time, one who is devoid of memory regarding the body or what transcends the body—
if he remembers even slightly— then he is endowed with everything.
Thus.
When even a minute degree of heterogeneity arises in the wise, there is no longer even non-attachment; how much less, then, the removal of veils?

Thus it is stated in the Śruti and by the teacher Gauḍapāda. For those who possess the delusion that the body and so forth exist as something separate from themselves, this "liberation while disembodied" (videhamukti) indeed occurs through the dissolution of the body from their perspective.

However, for those [who hold] that there exists the entire collection of the state of ignorance and its effects, characterized by a body and so forth as something separate from themselves—whether they say it exists or does not exist—[this liberation does not apply].
Even the expression of delusion partakes of negation;

at the very moment of the knowledge that Brahman alone exists—without a counter-correlate and established by the negation of that [delusion]—you, though appearing as if possessing bodies from the perspective of others, become indeed videhamukta (liberated while bodiless). There is no doubt in this matter.
Thus, it is established that there is dispute. And so says the Smṛti (p. 424):
"Alas! Pure Consciousness itself, through the conceit of 'I' and 'mine' regarding its own imagined body and so forth, assumes the state of a living being and wanders in saṃsāra as if bound."
If the body were to attain a state of mere appearance through one's own cognition,
then it would indeed manifest as pure consciousness, just like one who is liberated while living.
When the body and so forth do not manifest apart from one's own nature, then one becomes like one who has attained pure consciousness, the disembodied liberation (videhakaivalya).
May that which consists of one's own imagined body and so forth always shine by itself as pure consciousness alone;
for how could that which is pure consciousness ever become non-consciousness?
Thus [it is said].
In the present case, however, these things are disputed from the perspective of others; whether they exist or do not exist is irrelevant. 164.
Brahman is also in every respect [the reality]; the meaning is that just as there is no bubble or the like apart from water, so too there is no body or the like apart from Brahman.
A description of the microcosmic egg (piṇḍāṇḍa) as the abode of Śiva:
The body is a city with ten gates, possessing ten great thoroughfares in the form of channels (nāḍīs). || 165 ||
It is pervaded by the ten winds, bounded by the ten sense organs, possessing the six supports as its inner chambers, and the six lineages as its great forest. (166)
It is filled with the four seats (pīṭhas), illuminating the four traditions (āmnāyas);
it is the great liṅga of Bindu and Nāda, the abode of Śiva and Śakti. || 167 ||
The body is declared to be the abode of Śiva, bestowing perfection upon all embodied beings.

Having revealed the true nature of Brahman for those of the highest qualification, [the author] now reveals the extent of the microcosmic egg (piṇḍāṇḍa) for those of middling qualification, beginning with the verse "daśadvāra" (ten doors).
165–166 || "The lamp of the four traditions" (caturāmnāyadīpaka) means that which illuminates the four Vedas.
The "great liṅga of bindu and nāda": *bindu* is the mind (*manas*), and *nāda* is the intellect (*buddhi*).
It is the great liṅga that illuminates the existence and non-existence of the thousands of fluctuations (*vṛtti*) of those two. (p. 425)

That in which immediate consciousness resides is described as such; it is the abode of Śiva and Śakti, meaning that the body is the support for the *jīva-kuṇḍalī*. Thus, the body is said to be the temple of Śiva. || 167 || The body is proclaimed to be the dwelling place of Śiva.
The body is declared to be a temple; that individual soul is Śiva alone.
One should discard the floral offerings of ignorance and worship with the sense of "I am He."
Thus, from another scriptural passage.
An explanation of the six supports (ādhāras) and the four seats (pīṭhas):
The Mūlādhāra, which is triangular, is situated between the anus and the genitals. || 168 ||
They indeed declare that to be the abode of Śiva in the form of the individual soul (jīva), where the supreme power named Kuṇḍalinī is established. || 169 ||
From which wind arises, from which fire proceeds, from which the drop (bindu) arises, and from which the resonance (nāda) proceeds. || 170 ||
That from which the swan arises and from which the mind arises—this is the sacred seat (pīṭha) known as Kāmarūpa, which bestows the fruit of desire. || 171 ||
The wheel called Svādhiṣṭhāna is at the base of the penis and has six spokes;
the Maṇipūraka wheel is situated in the region of the navel and has ten spokes.
The great wheel with twelve spokes is also the unstruck (anāhata) [sound] within the heart;
O Lotus-born One, this is the sacred seat (pīṭha) known as Pūrṇagiri. 173.
O Lord of the Gods, the sixteen-spoked wheel called Viśuddhi, which is the sacred seat named Jālandhara, resides here in the pit of the throat.
(426) What is called Ājñā is the supreme two-petaled wheel between the eyebrows;
it is the great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha) known as Uḍḍiyāṇa, established above. 175.
The square [element] on the earth and so forth has Brahmā as its presiding deity;
the water, shaped like a half-moon, has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity.
The triangular mandala belongs to Fire; Rudra is its presiding deity.
The orb of Wind is hexagonal; Īśvara is its presiding deity.
The sphere of space is circular, and its presiding deity is Sadāśiva;
they know the sphere of the mind to be in the form of sound (nāda) between the eyebrows.
He explains the portion "the chamber with six supports" with the verse beginning *guda* (168–170).
He also explains the portion "filled with the four seats" with the verse beginning *tadetad* (171):
"The wise know 'I am Brahman'; one should always meditate eternally on the light-liṅga between the eyebrows."

According to the Vedic revelation, "He is the ascetic" (yati), he who knows the true nature of the microcosm (piṇḍāṇḍa) as the innermost Self (pratyag-ātman) is this sage who knows Brahman, the true nature of the macrocosm (brahmāṇḍa);
for there is oneness between the inner and outer consciousness, which is the substratum for the sublation of the phenomenal world in both its individual (vyaṣṭi) and collective (samaṣṭi) aspects.
The meaning is that one becomes one who has accomplished what was to be done. || 178 ||
Thus ends the first chapter.
The second chapter: The Qualification for the Knowledge of Yoga.
O Śaṅkara, I desire to hear once more the greatness of Yoga, by the mere knowledge of which one attains equality with the Khecarī [state]. || 1 ||
Listen, O Brahmin, I shall declare that which must be guarded with great effort:
he who performs service for twelve years without negligence. (2)
To him who is self-controlled and a celibate student, the teacher should speak according to the truth;
yet he who imparts it out of mere scholarship, greed for wealth, or negligence [is at fault]. (3)
By him everything has been studied and heard, and by him everything has been practiced—
by that wise one who knows the root mantra as revealed by the Guru.

Having thus heard the Yoga of Knowledge from the mouth of the Lord, the Four-faced One (Brahmā), as if still unsatisfied, again inquires about the majesty of the knowledge of Yoga; thus it is said: "Again...
[He] would become exceedingly radiant like the sun moving in the sky. || 1 || The Blessed One spoke the answer to the question:
"Listen," [he said]. (2) To him, he [taught] the vidyā which was about to be spoken by me. (3)

The meaning is that all of that is lost through the fault of imparting knowledge to one who is not qualified.
