He states [the following]—beginning with the word "mūla"—to show that if a qualified person understands correctly from the mouth of the Guru, he becomes one who has accomplished his purpose. 4.
The majesty of the root mantra known as the *praṇava*.
The mantra consisting of Śiva and Śakti has arisen from the Mūlādhāra;
O Brahmin, a listener or a speaker of that mantra is indeed difficult to find.
This is declared to be the sacred seat (pīṭha), the liṅga of sound (nādaliṅga) whose nature is my own;
by the mere knowledge of it, a person becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 6 ||
The sovereign powers (aiśvarya), such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, arise very soon.

He praises that mantra with the word "Śiva. That mantra must be either the Praṇava or the Nāda. Having realized its full extent, the speaker and the listener [think]: "I alone am the Supreme Lord. For it is not otherwise.
"There is no speaker or listener whatsoever other than myself who knows the limit of that [reality]. (5) He describes the true nature of that mantra:
"Because it is the substratum of all, it is the *pīṭha* (the sacred seat); for those who worship it, there is no cognition of a sign (*liṅga*) distinct from itself. (6)
That which gives is not the *nādaliṅga*. As for the question "Is that different from you?", [the answer is] "I alone am its self," meaning its essential nature (*svarūpa*);
thus it is "of my own nature" (*madātmaka*), because of the identity between the designation and the designated.
He states the fruit of knowing that [reality] with the words "Of that... (verse 6).
The definition of being the root-mantra is because of [the functions of] thinking and breathing, and because of the awakening to my own form. || 7 ||
O Brahmin, it is called "mantra" because it is my own abode,
because it is the root of all mantras, and because it arises from the mūlādhāra.
It is known as the "root-mantra" (mūlamantra) because it is the fundamental characteristic (liṅga) of its essential nature.
To the question, "Why does it possess the status of being the root-mantra? he says: "Because of thinking" (mananāt).
[The word] "mantram" is a transposition of case endings. It is just as all leaves are pierced by a single pin (śaṅku).
In the same way, all speech is woven together by the syllable Om; for, according to the Vedic revelation that "this whole world is indeed the syllable Om," it is the root. || 8 ||
The definition of the nature of the *nāda-liṅga* is due to its subtlety, its causality, its dissolution (*layana*), and its movement (*gamana*). || 9 ||
The Supreme Lord is designated as the *liṅga* because of His defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, He states that it possesses both the nature of a *liṅga* and the nature of a *sūtra* [in the verse beginning] "because of subtlety" (*sūkṣmatvāt*).
This is the definition of the nature of a *sūtra*.
And because of its constant presence among all living beings as well. || 10 ||
And because it indicates [the meaning], form is called a "sūtra.
(p. 429) The Praṇava has the Bindu as its seat;
she is Mahāmāyā, Mahālakṣmī, Mahādevī, and Sarasvatī. || 11 ||
The unmanifest foundational power (ādhāraśakti), by which the universe proceeds, exists in a subtle state as the drop (bindu) and in the form of the sacred seat (pīṭha). || 12 ||
Since the *praṇava* itself has been presented as the root mantra, the *liṅga*, and the *sūtra*, it possesses the nature of being the source (*prakṛtitva*).
This is because of the Vedic scripture which states: "The exponents of Brahman declare that its nature as the source arises from its being the *praṇava*.
To the question, "What is this source like?", he says: "She is Mahāmāyā" (verse 11). By her...
Through the nature of the *praṇava*, the universe proceeds as consisting of both the designator and the designated;

and she who is conventionally designated as Durgā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī is this very *ādhāra-śakti* (supporting power) whose form is unmanifest (*avyakta*). As to in what form she possesses both manifest and unmanifest aspects, it is the *bindu*; in that form, it is the mind (*manas*).
She is subtle and non-manifest; her grossness consists of the four seats (pīṭhas) beginning with Kāmarūpa. || 12 ||
The means for realizing the non-differentiated Brahman as the Praṇava is this:
having pierced through the seat of the Bindu, the Liṅga of Nāda is reached;
it is uttered by means of the vital breath, O Brahman, and by the process of "six-faced" articulation.
By means of the path of the teacher’s instruction, [the reality] shines forth all at once.

Thus, that which exists in the form of both the gross and the subtle—Brahman, established through the removal of the portions to be discarded within it—shines forth as devoid of distinctions by virtue of the teacher’s instruction; thus he says: "The Bindu," etc. O... (Note: The text provided ends with "he" and "O", suggesting an address to a disciple or interlocutor.)
O Brahman, that which is uttered as "Om" through the activity of the prāṇa, apāna, and vyāna breaths— that very [Om],

whose portion to be abandoned has been removed, whose seat is the Bindu, and which consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest, is [attained] by means of the path of the Guru's instruction through the process of "sixfold making," and— by the word "and"— by the sword of the knowledge of the undifferentiated Brahman.
For the yogi who has analyzed [reality] down to its very atoms, that which has arisen as the *nādaliṅga*—

characterized by the *bindu-pīṭha* transcending one's own self— is the fourth state of the fourth (*turyaturīya*). This is that which, whether the delusion of the waking-waking state and other such perceptions of one’s own ignorance exists or not, does not yield anything [different] throughout the three periods of time.
The meaning is that Brahman shines forth instantaneously as its own non-dual self alone. || 13 ||
(430) Brahman is threefold by way of its gross, subtle, and seed forms;
thus, the body of Brahman is threefold: as the gross, the subtle, and the supreme. || 14 ||
The gross form consisting of the five Brahmans is called Vairāja;
the subtle form of Hiraṇyagarbha, however, is the Nāda, which consists of the three seed-syllables.

He says "the gross" (sthūlam) [in verse 14] to explain that which remains as the Fourth of the Fourth (turyaturya), which manifests in three ways—as gross, subtle, and supreme—in accordance with the varying degrees of vision held by those beginning with the ignorant (svājña). Among these, the gross is fivefold; the other, however, is...

Regarding the word "hiraṇya": by the use of the particle *tu*, the consciousness of the seed (*bījacaitanya*) is also included; that, however, consists of the three seeds beginning with the letter Ā. || 15 ||
The pure reality is to be known solely through the practice of the self-mantra;
it is the supreme Brahman, the supreme truth, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss—immeasurable, indefinable, and beyond the reach of speech and mind. (16)
Pure, subtle, formless, changeless, stainless, infinite, indivisible, incomparable, and free from ailment. || 17 ||

Through the constant practice of the *ātman-mantra*, the supreme reality (*paratattva*) is revealed. He says that it is revealed as something superior to everything through the practice of the *ātman-mantra*, and not by itself—by which he means that the term "*ātman-mantra*" refers to the collection of the *praṇava* and the great sayings (*mahāvākya*). Having arisen from sleep...

Practice (*abhyāsa*) is the continuous engagement in hearing, reflection, and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*), in accordance with the Vedic injunction: "Let Brahman alone, which is the end of sleep, be thoroughly contemplated."
Listen to me regarding the signs of the manifestation of the supreme reality, the signs of that manifestation, and the gateways to supernatural powers.
The radiance of a lamp’s flame, the moon, fireflies, lightning, and the stars are seen in a subtle form by the yogin who is always disciplined. (19)
The sovereign powers (aiśvarya) such as atomization (aṇimā) arise for him without delay.
To the question, "What are the signs that manifest the direct realization of the supreme reality (paratattva)? he says: "That... [tad].
If the desire arises, then [powers such as] *aṇimā* and so forth [are attained].
There is no power equal to the majesty of the contemplation of *nāda*; there is no mantra higher than *nāda*, and no deity higher than one's own Self.
There is no worship higher than continuity, nor is there any happiness greater than contentment;
one who desires accomplishment should always guard this with great effort. (21)
He says that there is nothing equal to the satisfaction derived from the continuous contemplation of the nature of sound (nāda), stating: "There is none" (nāsti). || 20 ||
He states the necessity of concealing this mantra of one's own self, characterized by such specific attributes, because its meaning is an extreme secret: "It must be concealed."
The knowledge of the supreme reality arises only from devotion to the Guru and the Blessed Lord;
having realized this, my devotee becomes fulfilled and happy.
He who possesses supreme devotion for the Divine, and for the Guru as he does for the Divine—
For these subjects, when explained, become manifest to that high-souled one.
Thus [it is said].
He states the fruit of this knowledge: "My devotee," etc. (21).
He says "of whom" (yasya) to show that the aforementioned meaning is revealed only to one who possesses devotion toward the Śruti and the Teacher. || 22 ||
Thus ends the second chapter.
The third chapter: The fourfold forms of Nāda-Brahman, beginning with Parā and Paśyantī.
That which has been declared as the nameless, which is the cause of the supernatural powers, and by the mere knowledge of which one is liberated from the bondage of birth. || 1 ||
The imperishable, supreme sound is called Śabdabrahman;
it is the power residing in the Mūlādhāra, self-supported, and in the form of a drop (bindu).
Within that, the Nāda arises like a sprout from a subtle seed;
they know her as Paśyantī, by which yogis perceive the entire universe. (3)
In the heart, a sound is manifested resembling the roar of thundering clouds;
situated there, O Lord of the Gods, it is called the Middle (Madhyamā).
Furthermore, Vaikharī is manifested by means of *prāṇa*, which is termed "haste" (*tvarā*). Regarding that which was stated— that there is no mantra higher than *nāda*—
the third chapter is now commenced for the purpose of elaborating upon the expansion of Vaikharī.

Regarding the phrase "that which is to be saluted": in accordance with the Vedic scripture stating that "salutation signifies oneness," that which is to be saluted is that oneness which, having been realized by yogis, was declared to their own disciples as "there is nothing whatsoever apart from Consciousness. This is the point here.
One should contemplate: "This which exists here is consciousness alone; this is composed of consciousness and is indeed nothing but consciousness.
Consciousness is [the world], I am consciousness, and these worlds are consciousness."
Thus says the Śruti. That which is the source and ultimate consummation of all accomplishments,

simultaneous with the realization of pure consciousness alone— because the entire web of accomplishments has reached the state of non-accomplishment through that [realization]— is such that even an ignorant person, by means of mere knowledge, [is freed] from the delusion of anything other than the Self.
(p. 433) One is liberated from the delusion of what appears as other than oneself, which is a manifestation of one's own ignorance;
through the realization of one's own nature, by means of the dissolution of all else, one remains as oneself alone. Regarding this, there is a traditional teaching (*smṛti*):
"When that which arises from one's own ignorance—the appearance of what is other than oneself—has reached dissolution through the knowledge of one's own nature..."
Freed from all counter-correlates, only its own self remains.
Thus [ends the first section].

It has been stated that one is liberated through the knowledge of which; that [knowledge] is divided into two forms, higher and lower, based on the perspectives of those who know themselves (svajña) and others. To this he says: "The Imperishable" (*akṣaram*). Here, that which is experienced from the perspective of one who knows himself is the *akṣara*; the meaning is that it is the supreme, the highest *akṣara*.
However, that which is experienced through the vision of one's own ignorance is *nāda*, the nature of which is sound (*nādarūpa*);

it is the *śabdabrahman* (the Brahman of Sound) which serves as the means for attaining the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*), according to the Vedic scripture: "One who is proficient in the *śabdabrahman* attains the supreme Brahman. Now, where does this lower Brahman manifest? To this [it is said]:

He says: "The root. There exists a certain power (*śakti*) residing in the *mūlādhāra*, which is of the nature of universal consciousness (*citsāmānyātmikā*), unmanifest in form and known as the *bindu*, having *nāda* as its support.
In that very [power], *nāda* arises like the sprout from a subtle seed; this is the point.
In the *parā* state, it has become a sprout; in the *paśyantī* state, it is split into two petals;
in the *madhyamā* state, it is a bud; and in the *vaikharī* state, it is fully blossomed.

Thus says the Śruti. He states that they know her who is perceived as Parā to be Paśyantī and Vaikharī—namely, "tām" (her)—verse 3. That very sound (nāda), which has attained the state of a sprout within Parā residing in the Mūlādhāra, [manifests] in the heart as Paśyantī, known as Anāhata—verse 4. That same [sound], together with the vital breath (prāṇa) [becomes Madhyamā]—verse 5.
An explanation of the nature of the *vikharī*:
it takes the form of branches and sprouts due to the striking of the points of articulation, such as the palate and so forth. || 5 ||
One should utter the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa';
from the letters arise words, and from the words arises the formation of sentences.
All mantras consisting of speech, the Vedic scriptures in their entirety, the Purāṇas, the poetic works, and even the various spoken languages [are derived from it]. (7)
The seven musical notes and all the verses originate from sound;
this is the goddess Sarasvatī, who dwells within the secret cave of all beings. (8)
Propelled slowly by the wind joined with fire,
it always proceeds in this manner through sentences consisting of two or three syllables and words.
From the direct realization of Vaikharī comes the perfection of speech:
the yogi who perceives this Vaikharī power within his own self attains the perfection of speech through the grace of Sarasvatī. (10)
He will himself be the author of the Vedas, the Śāstras, and the Purāṇas. "Speech has four measured quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them."
Three [quarters] of speech are hidden in the cave and do not stir; humans speak only the fourth.
Thus, he states the fruit of the knowledge of Vaikharī as established by the Śruti, beginning with the words "yaḥ" (he who). || 10 ||
It is the nature of the supreme immutable, wherein reside the bindu and the nāda, as well as the moon, the sun, fire, and wind. || 11 ||
And all the sense organs, O observer of noble vows, go to dissolution where the vital breaths dissolve and where the mind dissolves. (12)
Having gained which, one considers no other gain to be superior to it;
established in which, one is not shaken even by heavy suffering. (13)
Where the mind, restrained through the practice of yoga, comes to rest;
and where, beholding the Self by means of the self, one finds satisfaction within the Self. (14)
That absolute bliss which is perceivable by the intellect and beyond the senses—this, being transcendent to both the perishable and the imperishable, is called the "Imperishable" (Anakṣara). || 15 ||
All beings are the perishable; the Sūtrātman is called the imperishable (akṣara). The supreme Brahman is the imperishable, devoid of distinctions and untainted.
It is without characteristics and cannot be characterized; it is beyond reasoning and incomparable. It is the shoreless shore, indivisible, inconceivable, and exceedingly pure.
The support of all beings, yet itself without support, free from affliction, immeasurable, indefinable, unfathomable, and beyond the reach of the senses. || 18 ||
It is neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long; it is unborn and undecaying, devoid of sound, touch, or form, and without eyes, ears, or name. 19.
Omniscient, all-pervading, and peaceful, it abides in the heart of all; it is easily realized through the grace of the Guru, yet extremely difficult for the mindless to understand. (20)
Partless, devoid of qualities, tranquil, changeless, and without support;
unstained, indestructible, immovable, unshakable, and eternal.

In response to the inquiry, "What is the supreme syllable (paramākṣara)?", he says "yatreti" (where...), meaning that which is the substratum of all negations, established by the absence of the state of being a substratum as determined by its own superimposed objects. [11] "Vāyo vāyavaḥ" [12–14]. The "syllable-less" (anakṣara) is the supreme syllable (paramākṣara).
15–19 || From the weightiness [of the teacher], that is, from the performance of the meaning taught by the teacher. 20–25 ||
Through devotion to and meditation upon the Śabdabrahman, there is the realization of the Supreme Brahman:
"It is the light even of lights, established beyond darkness;
it is free from existence and non-existence, and is the domain of pure contemplation alone. (22)
The supreme reality is accessible through devotion with a mind absorbed within;
O Lotus-born One, mere contemplation alone is the cause in this matter. (23)
Just as the mental impression (bhāvanā) is the cause for humans to attain another body,
so too the mind of a person contemplating an object finds delight in that very object.
For one who remembers me, the mind dissolves right here into me;
[therein lies] omniscience, supreme lordship, and the state of possessing all perfect powers.
"And the possession of infinite power shall arise from the remembrance of me.
Thus [it is said].
For those who, with a mind free from desire, worship the sound of the Brahman designated as Śabdabrahma,
there arises by the grace of Śabdabrahma that supreme reality which is the substratum of all negations,
which transcends the perishable and the imperishable, which is the "imperishable" (anakṣara), and so forth— that is, the reality which is without attributes and so on.
Thus, that which is distinguished by these specific attributes—the non-dual Brahman alone—becomes manifest as one's very self.
Since this is so, the meaning is that the relationship of means and end between the Śabdabrahman and the Parabrahman is established.
"Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end..."
To that very thing he goes, O son of Kuntī, being constantly permeated by the thought of it.

In accordance with this traditional teaching, just as contemplation (*bhāvanā*) alone is the cause for attaining another body, so too, those persons who worship Me in this world with a qualified or unqualified disposition (*bhāva*) become that very Brahman—qualified or unqualified—in accordance with the manner in which they meditate upon It. Thus: "In whatever way they worship Him... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1).
"It is exactly so," according to the sacred scripture (*śruti*). The word "iti" indicates the conclusion of the chapter.
Thus ends the third chapter.
The fourth chapter: The unreality of the state of being a living soul.
Since consciousness is of a single nature, no differentiation is ever logical;
likewise, the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) should be understood as being like the perception of a snake in a rope. || 1 ||
Just as a rope, through ignorance of its true nature, appears in an instant as a serpent,
so too does pure consciousness itself manifest directly in the form of the entire universe.

The entire collection of the state of ignorance and its effects, which are distinct from oneself and divided by various kinds of differences, is experienced as real by everyone. To the inquiry, "How then can that reach the state of non-existence even through a hundred meditations?"—the answer is: because it does not manifest from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*), that which is separate from oneself [is unreal].
It does not exist at all. For cultivation does not proceed toward a non-entity, such as the horn of a hare.

That which is the ultimate reality—the non-dual Brahman alone that remains—appears as if separate from itself to the vision of one who lacks self-knowledge. However, when [it is realized] through the knowledge of one's own Self...
When one's own ignorance is destroyed, from the perspective of ultimate reality, nothing remains apart from Brahman;

only Brahman alone remains. To elaborate upon this meaning, the fourth chapter begins with the words "caitanyasya" (of consciousness). This refers to the consciousness that pervades all things, like the space that permeates a jar, a bowl, and so forth.
Regarding the claim that "the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) is real," he provides an answer with an illustration: "The state of being a living soul... (verse 1).

Since the world is perceived as something distinct from Brahman, it might be thought that it is real; however, because its existence is limited by one's own ignorance, that world becomes consciousness alone upon the arising of self-knowledge.
He states this with an illustration: "Due to the ignorance of the rope," etc. (Verse 2).
Brahman is the material cause of all phenomenal manifestation; there exists nothing other than Brahman that constitutes the manifestation.
Therefore, this entire phenomenal world is Brahman alone, and nothing else. || 3 ||
The relationship between the pervaded and the pervader is false, according to the teaching that "all is the Self.
When the supreme reality is thus known, how can there be any occasion for duality? (4)
All beings are born from Brahman, the Supreme Self;
therefore, contemplate that these [beings] are indeed Brahman itself. (5)
Contemplate this: Brahman alone sustains all names, various forms, and all actions without exception.
Just as that which is born from gold possesses the eternal nature of gold,
so too does that which is born from Brahman possess the nature of Brahman.

Observing one who thinks that the phenomenal world exists because of the reality of the conceptualization of cause and effect, or the pervaded and the pervader, he says: "The material cause," etc. Since it is so, therefore [the conclusion follows]. (3–4)

He states, with an illustration, that the collection of elements (bhūtajāta) is indeed that very Brahman, on the grounds that it is the effect of Brahman—just like name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and action (karman)—in the passage beginning with "of Brahman" (brahmaṇaḥ). Why?
Because [it arises] from Brahman. Furthermore: "Brahman alone" (6); "as from gold" (7).
Because of perceiving [the Self] as distinct from Brahman, one incurs misfortune;
for it is said that fear exists even for that deluded soul who stands apart, making even the slightest distinction between the individual self (jīvātman) and the Supreme Self (paramātman). (8)
Due to ignorance, duality arises; otherwise, one perceives everything as the Self, and there is not even an atom of anything else therein.

The text states "even a little" (*svalpam*) to describe the harm that comes to one who perceives even the slightest thing as separate from Brahman. The meaning is that fear is also proclaimed by another Vedic scripture: "For when he makes even a slight distinction within this [Brahman], then fear arises for him. [Verse 8] This [world-appearance] is a manifestation of one's own ignorance.
He says that non-duality appears as duality due to one's own ignorance: "That which... (verse 9).
The falsity of the phenomenal world of conventional experience is as follows:
although this world is experienced and remains capable of practical function, it is of the nature of reality [only in appearance], just like a dream that is sublated in the subsequent moment. (10)
In dream there is no waking state, and in waking there is indeed no dream-state;
both of these do not exist in deep sleep (laya), nor does even that deep sleep exist for these two.
The triad itself would be false, being composed of the three qualities;
its witness is beyond the qualities, eternal, and indeed of the nature of consciousness.

Just as the delusion of a jar in clay or the perception of silver in mother-of-pearl ceases when one perceives the underlying reality, so too the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) vanishes when Brahman is truly beheld. (13)
Just as when there is a jar in clay, or the designation "earring" in gold,
or the appearance of silver in mother-of-pearl, so too is the referent of the word "individual soul" (jīva) in the Supreme.
Just as there is blueness in the sky, as there is water in a desert, and as there is the nature of a person in a post, so too is the universe [superimposed] upon the conscious Self. 15.
Just as a ghost is empty, just as the city of the Gandharvas, and just as there is the appearance of two moons in the sky, so too is the existence of the world within reality. 16.
Just as water alone manifests intensely through waves and billows, as the earth is designated by the name "pot," and as threads are designated by the name "cloth. (17)
By the name of the world, it is Brahman alone that shines as consciousness; everything is indeed only Brahman.
(p. 440) To one who considers that which is distinct from itself to possess empirical reality, he says:
"It is experienced" (anubhūta). || 10 || [He thus addresses] the mutual variability of the states of waking and so forth.

He states the eternity of the substratum for that conceptualization in the verse beginning with "svapne" (11-12). He explains, along with an illustration, that the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) and so forth is limited by the knowledge of the true nature of what is other than oneself, in the verse beginning with "yadvat" (13).
The absolute non-existence of the phenomenal world as something separate from oneself is like this:
just as the son of a barren woman does not exist, and just as there is no water in a desert. 18.
Just as there is no tree in the sky, so there is no abiding reality of the world;
for just as when a jar is perceived, it is only clay that appears by force.

When the phenomenal world (prapañca) is scrutinized, it is Brahman alone that shines forth resplendent. What more need be said? He states the absolute impossibility of a phenomenal world apart from that [Brahman] with the words "yathā" (just as).
The superimposition of the body and so forth upon the Self is produced by ignorance;
for although the Self is eternally pure, it indeed always appears as impure. (20)
Just as the rope is perceived in two ways by the ignorant and the wise respectively, and just as there is the clay pot, so too is the body composed of consciousness. 21.
This discrimination between the self and the non-self is performed by the wise in vain, just as a rope [is mistaken] for a serpent or mother-of-pearl for silver. (22)
The nature of the Self has been determined as being the body by the deluded person, just as the earth is [mistakenly] perceived as a jar or a mirage as water. (23)
For just as wood is perceived as a house and iron as a sword, so too does one perceive "bodiness" in the Self through the power of ignorance. (24)
Thus [it is said].

Since it is thus, therefore [it is said] "always" (sadaiva). || 20-21 || That being so, [the text says] "the Self" (ātman) and so forth; because that which is non-Self is difficult to obtain [in its true nature], as if it were a serpent. || 22-23 || But in reality, the established meaning is that Brahman—established through the negation of everything—is indeed without a counterpart (niṣpratiyogika). || 24 || The word "iti" signifies the completion of the chapter.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.
The fifth chapter:
The Body as the Abode of Viṣṇu.
I shall further proclaim the secret yoga whose nature is Brahman; O Brahmin, listen with a concentrated mind according to the proper sequence. (1)
The body is a city of ten gates, with the ten channels as its great highways;
it is pervaded by the ten vital airs and furnished with the ten sense organs as its appendages.
It has the six supports as its inner chambers and the six lineages as its great forest;
it is filled with the four seats and illuminated by the four traditions.

The body is declared to be the abode of Viṣṇu, the temple of Viṣṇu, which contains the great liṅgas of Bindu and Nāda, and is the dwelling place of Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī; it bestows perfection upon all embodied beings.

Having thus established the non-differentiated Brahman for those of the highest capacity, the fifth chapter is now commenced with the words "Again" (punar), because yoga—which was previously mentioned for those of intermediate capacity—must be explained once more along with its various methods by the teachers of yoga. 1–2. By the teachers of yoga.
By means of the different lineages of the oral traditions (*sampradāya*)— namely, Mantra, Laya, Haṭha, Rāja, Bhāvanā, and Sahaja Yoga— beginning with Bhusuṇḍa and others,
the "Great Forest" (*mahāvana*) is that in which these very six lineages (*ṣaḍanvaya*) exist; thus it is so described, for each one [of them].
Because the lineage (anvaya) is as boundless as the ocean. || 3 || Previously, it was stated that [this place] is the abode of Śiva and Śakti, the temple of Śiva;

furthermore, the statement that it is the abode of Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī, the temple of Viṣṇu, should be understood as being for the purpose of dispelling the delusion of difference between Śiva and Viṣṇu. || 4–15 ||
An explanation of the six supports (ādhāras) and the four seats (pīṭhas):
The Mūlādhāra, triangular in shape, is situated between the anus and the genitals;
they indeed declare that to be the abode of Śiva in his form as the individual soul (jīva). || 5 ||
Therein is established the supreme power named Kuṇḍalinī,
from which wind arises and from which fire proceeds.
From which the bindu arises, from which the nāda proceeds, from which the haṃsa is produced, and from which the mind is born. || 7 ||
This very seat (pīṭha), known as Kāmarūpa, bestows the fruit of desires;
it is the wheel (cakra) called Svādhiṣṭhāna, located at the base of the liṅga and having six spokes.
The ten-spoked Maṇipūraka wheel is situated at the region of the navel,
and the great twelve-spoked Anāhata wheel is also located in the heart.
O Lotus-born One, this sacred seat named Pūrṇagiri is that sixteen-spoked wheel called Viśuddha which is located in the throat-pit.
O Four-faced One, the seat named Jālandhara is situated here;
the supreme two-petaled wheel called Ājñā is located between the eyebrows.
The great seat (pīṭha) called Uḍḍiyāṇa is established above.
These locations within this body manifest as the nature of Śakti. (12)
The earth and so forth are square; Brahmā is their presiding deity.
Water is semicircular in shape; Viṣṇu is its presiding deity.
The triangular maṇḍala belongs to Fire; Rudra is its presiding deity.
The orb of Wind, however, is hexagonal; Saṃkarṣaṇa is the presiding deity here.
The sphere of space is circular; the illustrious Nārāyaṇa is its presiding deity. They know the sphere of the mind to be in the form of sound, located between the eyebrows. (15)
"O Lotus-born one, this state of Śambhu has been described to you. He says "Śāmbhava" because this was stated for the most part at the end of the first chapter.
Hereafter, I shall explain the nature of the network of channels (nāḍīcakra) and the definitive determination of that network of channels. || 16 ||
Situated at the triangle of the *mūlādhāra*, twelve finger-breadths long, and resembling a bamboo stalk cut at its base, it is known as the *brahmanāḍī*. (17)
The Iḍā and the Piṅgalā proceed along its two sides;
they are woven through the Vilambinī and extend as far as the end of the nāḍikā.
In the iḍā, the wind moves through the left side in the form of mercury;
in the piṅgalā, however, the solar self moves from the right side. (19)
The channel called Vilambinī is clearly established at the navel;
from there, channels have arisen facing sideways, upwards, and downwards. (20)
That is called the navel-wheel (nābhicakra), situated like a hen’s egg;
from there, the two channels Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā proceed to the two eyes. (21)
Pūṣā and Ālambusā have reached the two ears;
the great channel named Śūrā is situated there, extending from them to the middle of the eyebrows.
The channel known as Viśvodarī consumes the four kinds of food,
while the channel known as Sarasvatī extends to the tip of the tongue.
The channel called Rākā, however, having drunk water for a moment,
causes sneezing in the nose and accumulates phlegm.
The channel named Śaṅkhinī, originating from the pit of the throat and facing downwards,
constantly takes up the essence of food and accumulates it in the head.
There are three channels extending downward from the navel, facing downwards:
the *kuhū* channel expels waste matter, and the *vāruṇī* releases urine.
The channel named Citrā is the "sewer," which causes the discharge of semen;
this is declared to be the wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra). Now, hear about that which is in the form of the drop (bindu). || 27 ||
Next, he describes the essential nature of the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) with the words "from this" (*ataḥ*). (16–27)
The body of Brahman consists of the three principles of Bindu, Agni, and Soma;
the form of Brahman is threefold, namely the gross, the subtle, and the supreme.
The gross is the white Bindu, while the subtle has the nature of the five fires. (28)
The Supreme is declared to be of the nature of Soma, the eternal witness, ever-unfallen;
he is the embodiment of the five fires, beginning with the fire of cosmic destruction. (28)
The meditation on the five fires and its fruit:
in the lower region of the netherworlds (pātāla), there resides the Fire of Time (kālāgni). || 29 ||
That root-fire is the fire within the body from which *nāda* is produced;
indeed, the *vaḍavāgni* (submarine fire) resides in the body and operates within the marrow of the bones.
For fire exists within wood and stone, as well as within the marrow of bones;
the fire born of wood and stone is of the earth element and resides in the *grahaṇī*. || 31 ||
The fire of lightning, whose essence is within itself, resides in the intermediate space;
the fire in the form of the sun is situated in the sky, resting upon the circle of the navel.
That sun rains down poison, while facing upward it flows with nectar;
the moon, situated at the root of the palate, faces downward and rains down ambrosia.
The Bindu, residing in the middle of the eyebrows, resembling pure crystal—that is said to be the subtle form of the divine Mahāviṣṇu. || 34 ||
The wise person who meditates upon this form of the five fires with their intellect—whatever they eat and whatever they drink has been offered as an oblation; of this there is no doubt.

He describes the nature of the five fires in sequence, beginning with the words "of the Pātālas. This refers to the Pātālas, the worlds ending with Pātāla, starting from Atala. (29) Kālāgni itself, having become the fire that supports the *nāda*, resides within the body. (30) Likewise, [as stated] "like wood," it is situated in the *grahaṇī*.
He states the fruit of the meditation on the five fires: "This," etc. (verse 35).

Having first performed purification of the body, one who has comfortably mastered the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī, who is well-accustomed to sleep, and who eats food that is well-digested and moderate, should assume a comfortable posture. (36)
One should purify the path of the vital breath through exhalation, inhalation, and retention;
contracting the anus with effort, one should worship the Mūla-śakti. || 37 ||

Thus, one attains purification of the body through diet. That posture by which one's own ease is maintained is the "easy" (sukha) posture. [36] One should worship the Root Power; the meaning is that one should awaken the Kuṇḍalinī power. [37–42]
The practice of Khecarīmudrā and its fruit: One should bind the lock known as Uḍḍiyāṇa between the navel and the genitals;
by means of that, the Śakti flies up to the seat of Uḍḍiyāṇa. (38)
One should slightly contract the throat; this indeed is the Jālandhara Bandha.
With a firm mind and concentrated focus, one should bind the Khecarī Mudrā. (39)
The tongue enters the cavity of the skull and moves in reverse;
the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows—this is the Khecarī mudrā. (40)
By whomsoever the aperture above the uvula is sealed by the Khecarī [mudrā], the nectar does not fall into the fire, nor does the vital wind rush forth. (41)
Neither hunger, nor thirst, nor sleep, nor even laziness arises;
and death shall not come to him who knows the Khecarī Mudrā. 42.

Through the meditation on Nārāyaṇa within the thousand-spoked [lotus], the attainment of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) occurs; thence, in the eastern and western void, in the twelve-finger space (*dvādaśānta*) whose nature is the Infallible One (*acyuta*), in the sacred seat of Uḍḍiyāṇa, which is free from duality, without support, and stainless. (43)
Then, one should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa, situated in the midst of a lotus and within the orb of the moon, constantly pouring forth nectar.
The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut away, and one's karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen. 45.

Then, meditating upon Nārāyaṇa—who is his own self—as the one from whom nectar flows in the space of the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*), or in the *ājñā* [cakra], the yogi attains the perfection of liberation (*kaivalya*), which is the impossibility of knots, doubt, and karma. Thus he says: "Then... (verses 43–45).

Now, O Lord of the Gods, I shall proclaim the means for attaining those various accomplishments for one engaged in the aforementioned meditation— a method that is easy to practice for those who have conquered their senses, who are tranquil, and who have mastered their breath and their minds. (46)
O Brahman, by dissolving the mind in the *nāda*, one gains the power of hearing from afar;
by dissolving the mind in the *bindu*, one attains the power of seeing from afar. (47)
When the mind is dissolved into the self of Time (Kālātman), it becomes the cause of knowledge of the three times.
Through the union of one's own mind with another's body, one effects entry into that other body. 48.
One should contemplate nectar at the crown of the head for the pacification of hunger, thirst, and poison;
one should fix the mind upon the earth, and there will be the ability to go to the netherworld (pātāla). (49)
One should fix the mind upon water; it is not overwhelmed by water.
One should fix the mind upon fire; it is not burned by fire. (50)
One should effect the dissolution of the mind in the air, and the power of traveling through the sky will arise;
one should fix the consciousness in space, and one shall attain the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
By yoking the mind to the form of Virāj, one attains greatness;
by yoking the mind to the Four-faced One, one becomes a creator of the world. (52)
Meditating upon himself as having the form of Indra, he enjoys mortal pleasures;
as a great yogi in the form of Viṣṇu, he protects the entire world.
In the form of Rudra, the great yogi indeed withdraws [all] by means of his splendor.
By yoking the mind to Nārāyaṇa, one becomes identical with Nārāyaṇa;
by yoking the mind to Vāsudeva, one attains all perfections.
Just as a yogi, disciplined in yoga and having conquered his senses, may resolve, so he attains each respective thing; indeed, intention alone is the cause in this matter.
To him who meditates in this manner, he says, "I shall describe the various means for attaining supernatural powers (siddhi)":
"Now" (atha) [verse 46]. "In the bindu, the eyes, the pupils" [verses 47–61].
The Ritual for Worshipping the Guru:
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, and the Guru is the eternal, infallible God.
There exists no one superior to the Guru within the three worlds. (56)
One should worship with supreme devotion the Preceptor, the Supreme Lord, who is the instructor of divine knowledge; through that, the fruit of knowledge shall be attained. (57)
As is the Guru, so is the Lord; as is the Lord, so is the Guru.
He is to be worshipped with great devotion; no difference exists between these two.
One should never maintain a doctrine of non-duality with one's guru;
rather, one should with devotion contemplate the non-duality of the guru, the deity, and oneself. (59)
The Great-Minded One who knows the greatness of the Yoga-Śikhā, that great secret of the Yoga-Śikhā—
for him there is nothing unknown throughout the three worlds. (60)
In this circle of saṃsāra, there is neither merit nor sin, neither ill health, nor suffering, nor defeat; nor is there any returning again. 61.
Regarding the methods for attaining supernatural powers (siddhis), one should not set the mind upon such success due to the fickleness of the mind;
nevertheless, he who has realized the true nature of reality is indeed liberated—of this there is no doubt. (62)
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.

The meaning is that for yogins who have realized the true nature of their own self, there is neither loss nor gain whatsoever, regardless of whether their spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*) are concealed or not. Thus, the word "Upaniṣad" marks the conclusion of the fifth chapter. || 62 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter.
The sixth chapter:
The method of worship of the Kuṇḍalinī-śakti.
O Supreme Lord, tell me the method of worship by which, through mere knowledge of it, one becomes liberated from worldly existence. || 1 ||
O Hiraṇyagarbha, I shall declare to you the method of worship—a secret that is the essence of the Vedas; having heard it, perform the worship correctly.
Salutations to you, Suṣumnā, Kuṇḍalinī, and Sudhā; from the lunar sphere, salutations to Manonmanī, the Great Power, whose essence is consciousness.

The four-faced Brahmā asks Maheśvara, "Tell me the method of practicing the means by which the world of those ignorant of their own true nature is liberated," as expressed in the verse beginning with "Upāsanā" (1).
The Blessed One spoke the answer to the question: "Upāsanā" (verse 2). He then described the mantra for that worship, its method, and its fruit: "Of Suṣumnā" (verse 3).
The nature of the *suṣumnā*:
there are one hundred and one channels of the heart; among them, one extends upward to the crown of the head.
Going upwards by that [path], one attains immortality; the others depart in various directions by way of transmigration. || 4 ||
Among those, one hundred and one channels are known as supreme;
the Suṣumnā is merged in the Supreme, while the Virajā is of the nature of Brahman.
The *iḍā* stands on the left, while the *piṅgalā* is on the right;
between these two is the supreme place—he who knows that is a knower of the Veda.
One should sustain the vital breaths moving within the nostrils therein;
having established the breath there, one should practice very gradually. (7)
In this region at the back of the anus, O bearer of the body, is the spinal column;
extending as a long bone throughout the body, it is called the Brahma-nāḍī.
At its end is a subtle cavity called the *brahmanāḍī* by the wise;
between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* lies the *suṣumnā*, which has the form of the sun.
He states the form of the *suṣumṇā* and the fruit of traveling along that path in verse 4-15: "A hundred... etc.
The Suṣumnā is the support of all; everything is established in it, which is all-pervading and faces every direction.
Within its center reside the Sun, the Moon, Fire, and the Supreme Lord.

The earth, the worlds, the directions, the fields, the oceans, the mountains, the rocks, the islands, the rivers, the Vedas, the scriptures, the sciences, the arts, and the syllables—[all these arose]. (11)

The vowels, mantras, Purāṇas, and these qualities in their entirety—of these, the seed is that which consists of the seed; the individual souls (kṣetrajñas) are the vital breaths (prāṇavāyus). || 12 ||
The universe is contained within the Suṣumnā; everything is established in that, which resides within the inner self of all beings and flows through the various channels.
With its roots above and branches below, all-pervading through the path of the vital air,
there are seventy-two thousand channels that are the domain of the vital air.
By means of every path, the lateral channels are hollow and of a porous nature;
and below and above the Kuṇḍalī, all the gates [of the senses] are blocked.

By awakening the supreme power (*parāśakti*) together with the vital wind (*vāyu*), and through the upward-moving knowledge of the individual soul (*jīva*), one attains liberation. Having known the *suṣumnā* and having pierced it, one should direct the anus toward the middle [channel]. (16)
Having performed [this] at the location of the bindu, one should restrain [the breath] in the nostrils;
there are seventy-two thousand gateways of the channels within the cage [of the body].
Suṣumnā is the Śāmbhavī power; all others are indeed useless.
Hṛllekhā, who resides at the root of the palate, is supreme bliss. (18)

Beyond this, however, in the state of cessation (nirodha), one should utter the middle [vowel] and the middle-middle [vowel], the supreme power (parā śakti) residing in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
If there is the creation of bees [within that state], one shall abandon the wandering of saṃsāra. || 19 ||

The "vital power" (jīvaśakti) means Kuṇḍalinī. || 16 || "In the place of the Bindu" means in the middle of the eyebrows; "in the cage" means in the body. || 17 || In the Hṛllekhā, which is expressed by the syllable Hrīṃ, in supreme bliss, in the principle of Īśvara situated at the root of the palate, one should restrain the mind and the other faculties. || 18 || The "middle" is the fourth state (turīya).
The middle-middle [state] is the fourth-of-the-fourth; having made that the object of focus, one should utter it—one should utter the nature of the *praṇava* for the duration of sixteen *mātrās*.
[It is] the one dwelling in the aperture of Brahmā—the *mātrā* that completes the number sixteen.

Because it is the seat of the *brahmarandhra* by virtue of being the supreme ground (*parābhūmi*). Regarding the phrase "there, if": the "bee" (*bhramara*) is the multitude of mental fluctuations such as desire and volition, which wanders about after conceptualizing what is other than itself;
[as stated: "desire, volition, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear."

Because of the Vedic scripture stating, "All this is indeed the mind alone," its creation would be a mental construction (*kalpanā*). However, in that [state], there is never any occasion for such construction, because the *brahmarandhra* is devoid of causal seeds (*nirbījatvāt*).
If, on the other hand, having reached the region below the midpoint of the eyebrows, the creation of desire, volition, and so forth occurs in the *viśuddhi-cakra*...

At that time, having seized the wheel of command (ājñācakra), one should—through fortitude—abandon and negate the cause of one's own misfortune, namely the wandering in saṃsāra, which is the wandering among objects perceived as separate from oneself; for there is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from one’s own self. This is the meaning. || 19 ||

I behold Your supreme self-meditation, which abides in coming and going yet is devoid of movement and the like; a lamp of the nature of consciousness amidst the darkness of ignorance; situated within all people—homage to You, the *haṃsa*, whose form is the supreme self. (20)
Of that unstruck sound (anāhata), there is its resonance (dhvani);
within the resonance is the light, and within the light is the mind.
That mind dissolves away; that is the supreme state of Viṣṇu.

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "It goes" (*gama*). [The Self] is devoid of the movement of the entire collection of its own internal organ's modifications (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti-kadamba*), because in reality there is an absence of any internal organ distinct from itself and its effects; therefore, it is devoid of going and so forth. From that...

It is called the "Lamp of Consciousness" (cadrūpadīpa) because it illuminates the darkness of ignorance that is other than itself with the flame of the fire of the nature of consciousness, reducing it to mere ashes. The remainder is clear. || 20 ||

The meaning is that the station of Viṣṇu remains as the only residue— established by the awakening of the impossibility of the mind along with its functions, which is characterized by the manifestation of the light of sound arising from the Mūlādhāra (the unstruck sound) up to the Vaikharī stage. || 21 ||

Some say that liberation results from the dissolution of the vital breaths and other elements into the foundational Brahman; they also state that the foundation consists of the Suṣumnā and Sarasvatī, for from this foundation the universe is born and into it the universe dissolves. (22)
Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge at the feet of the Guru;
for through the sleep of the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti), the universe comes into being by means of that sleep.
Through the awakening of that power, the three worlds awaken;
he who understands the support attains that which is beyond darkness.
By the mere knowledge of this, a person is liberated from sins. || 25 ||
By the light of the *ādhāra-cakra*, possessing a radiance like a mass of lightning, there is then liberation without a doubt, provided that the Guru himself is pleased. (26)
By the radiance of the *ādhāra-cakra*, one should sever both merit and sin;
through the obstruction of the *ādhāra-vāta*, [the breath] dissolves within the expanse of the sky.
Just as the body trembles due to the obstruction of the foundational wind (ādhāra-vāta), so too the yogi dances perpetually due to the obstruction of the foundational wind;
and due to the obstruction of the foundational wind, the entire universe is perceived right there. || 28 ||
The creation, the support, the support of supports, and all the deities reside in the support;
all the Vedas also reside in the support. Therefore, one should take refuge in the support. || 29 ||
In the western part of Ādhāra, there is the confluence of the Triveṇī;
by bathing and drinking there, a person is liberated from sin. || 30 ||
In the foundation lies the western linga; there a door-panel exists.
By merely opening it, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence. || 31 ||
If the moon and sun are fixed in the western part of the foundation, the Lord of the Universe resides there; by meditating upon Him, one becomes identical with Brahman.

Some say that liberation consists in abiding in the nature of the supportless Brahman, characterized by the dissolution of the *nāda*, the *ādhāra*, the *prāṇa*, and so forth, due to the absence of anything to be supported [by them].
He states that this too is indeed logical, saying "some": [the two channels] Suṣumṇā and Sarasvatī are established where [the central channel is located].

The meaning is that it is the root-support (mūlādhāra). He also states its status as the substratum for the superimposition and negation of the universe by way of its nature as Brahman: "from the support," etc. (22). Since this is so, therefore, he by whom the true nature of the root-support is shown is the Guru, who is the Supreme Self.
Because it liberates one from one's own ignorance, one should take refuge in that state, which is its very nature. Furthermore, regarding the term "support" (*ādhāra*):
the support-power (*ādhāraśakti*) is Kuṇḍalinī; her abiding in her own support is "sleep," and while that sleep exists—

The universe becomes characterized by the sleep of one's own ignorance. Its awakening, however, is the entry into the *suṣumnā*. Through that, the realization of the true nature of the three worlds arises. Thus, he states the fruit of such knowledge: "The support," etc. [24–25]. Of liberation.
Because it is obtainable solely through the grace of the Guru, according to the Vedic scripture: "He alone whom this [Self] chooses, by him is He obtained."

Furthermore—regarding the term "substratum" (ādhāra): the meaning is that the universe is perceived in that very [consciousness] alone, and does not appear as something separate from itself. || 27–28 || As for how it functions as a substratum:
because the creation, which is distinct from itself, proceeds by depending upon its own substratum; for in the absence of that [substratum], it would not exist. || 29 ||
Since it is possible [for all things to exist therein], it is established that Brahman is the substratum and the foundation of all.

How so? In this regard: "When the substratum exists, all the deities [reside there]. (29) The triple braid consists of Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā. (30) The western liṅga is the inward-facing consciousness; its door-panel is the obscuring [veil]."
The three knots [are located] in the western part of the Ādhāra, within the Suṣumnā. || 31-32 ||
By meditating on the forms of Brahmā and the others within the wheels (cakras), there is entry into the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
A form exists by its name in the western part of the foundation (ādhāra);
having pierced the six wheels, it has gone out from the aperture of Brahmā.
Restraining [the breath] in the left and right [channels], they enter through the suṣumṇā;
having entered the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), they attain the supreme goal. || 34 ||

The form of Brahmā and the other deities is as follows: thus the practitioners, preceded by meditation on the forms that adorn each respective cakra, [contemplate] the six cakras. First, the yogin [should withdraw] the vital breath (prāṇa) that previously had gone outside from the aperture of Brahmā—that is, the aperture of the *suṣumnā*—into the left and right [channels].

The *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* are restrained; that is, they bring about cessation. Then, those vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth suddenly pierce the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) adorned with the three knots of the *suṣumnā*, taste the nectar born from the unification of the moon, sun, and fire, and [attain] the fourth state (*turīya*) shining within the thousand-spoked wheel.
Or they enter that which transcends the fourth [state], namely the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), those who do so in this manner. 33–34.

Liberation belongs to one whose senses have dissolved into the aperture of Brahmā when the *haṃsa* runs up and down the *suṣumnā*. When one causes the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to circulate incessantly within the *suṣumnā*, [liberation is attained]. (35)
When the vital breath of the wise becomes steady within the Suṣumnā, the Moon and the Sun reach dissolution by entering the Suṣumnā. (36)
At that time, he who knows the state of equal flavor (samarasa) is a knower of Yoga;
when the rush of the mind dies away within the Suṣumnā, he is such a one.
When the yogi remains in the suṣumnā for even a single moment;
when the yogi abides in the suṣumnā for half a moment. (38)
When the yogi is firmly fixed within the Suṣumnā like salt in water, when the yogi merges into the Suṣumnā like milk and water; (39)
Then the knot is split asunder, all doubts are severed;
they are dissolved in the supreme ether and they attain the highest goal.

He says that those for whom the sheath of the organs dissolves into the aperture of Brahman (*brahmarandhra*) through the gateway of the *suṣumnā* become liberated—thus: "In the *suṣumnā*. *Haṃsa* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). (Verses 35–39).
He states the fruit of the dissolution in the *suṣumnā* thus: "It is split. The knot of the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). (Verse 40).

Having bathed in the Gaṅgā and the ocean and having bowed to Maṇikarṇikā, the greatness of the yoga of Suṣumnā does not equal even a sixteenth part of the investigation into the central channel (madhyanāḍī). 41.
Liberation comes from beholding Śrīśaila, from dying in Vārāṇasī, from drinking the water of Kedāra, and from the manifestation of the central channel (madhyanāḍī). || 42 ||
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the yoga of meditation on the Suṣumṇā.
When any man holds a gathering within the Suṣumnā,
he is liberated from all sins and shall attain the supreme good.
Suṣumṇā alone is the supreme sacred ford; Suṣumṇā alone is the supreme recitation;
Suṣumṇā alone is the supreme meditation; Suṣumṇā alone is the supreme goal. || 45 ||
Numerous sacrifices, gifts, vows, and observances do not equal even a sixteenth part of the yoga of meditation upon the Suṣumṇā. (46)
He praises the investigation of the *suṣumnā* and so forth with the verse beginning "In the Gaṅgā" (41–46).
The distinction between the locations of the power of consciousness (cicchakti) and the individual soul (jīva):
The supreme goddess Cicchakti always resides in the great place, the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), well-established in the center. (47)
The power of Māyā is likewise in the lotus of space at the tip of the forehead;
the supreme power, in the form of Nāda, is in the middle of the forehead.
In the posterior portion of the forehead, the power consisting of the *bindu* resides;
and within the *bindu*, the individual soul (*jīvātman*) exists in a subtle form. (49)
It exists in the heart in a gross form, but not in the middle channel.

In locations such as the *brahmarandhra* and others, the powers of consciousness (*cicchakti*) and so forth reside; within the *bindu* and other centers, the individual soul (*jīva*) also resides. This very soul, failing to attain rest due to the influence of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths, remains intent on the silent recitation (*japa*) of the *haṃsa* under the guise of the activity of exhalation and inhalation.
He says that it "becomes" at the *brahmarandhra* and in the center between the eyebrows. || 47 ||
And likewise, it exists in the space of the heart; this is to be supplied [to the previous verse]. It consists of the *bindu* and has the nature of the mind.

49 || The individual soul (jīva) exists in the form of a gross body within the middle [of the heart], but not in the "middle" [of the eyebrows]; nor does the soul migrate to the thousand-petalled lotus (sahasrāra). If it were to go to the space between the eyebrows and so forth, then it would become either the perishable (kṣara) or the supreme imperishable (paramākṣara); this is the meaning. 50 ||
The method of reciting the Haṃsa-mantra for the individual soul (jīva) under the influence of the vital breath (vāyu):
"The individual soul, subject to the control of prāṇa and apāna, indeed rushes up and down;
because of its flickering nature, it is not perceived through the left and right channels. (51)
Just as a ball, when struck by the staff-like arm,
rises upward, so too the individual soul, impelled by the prāṇa and apāna breaths, finds no rest.
The apāna draws up the prāṇa, and the prāṇa draws up the apāna;
by the sound "ha" it goes out, and by the sound "sa" it enters again.
The individual soul (jīva) constantly mutters this mantra, "haṃsa, haṃsa.
He who knows that eternal syllable is a knower of yoga.

"This very one, [consisting of] prāṇa and apāna"—by what path does he run until he is no longer seen? To this, [the answer is] "on the left. (51) He states the illustration for its movement: "thrown" and so forth.

52 || How is that? "By the letter *ha*. || 53 || Even though the individual soul (*jīva*) is of such a nature, by casting off its own inherent state of being a *jīva* through the knowledge "I am the Imperishable" (*akṣara*), it becomes that very [Imperishable]; thus he says: "That. || 54 ||
(459) Due to the distinction between the states of Kuṇḍalinī, the arrangement of bondage and liberation is as follows:
Above the *kanda*, the power Kuṇḍalinī is the form of liberation for yogins, yet she leads to bondage for the deluded; he who knows her is a knower of yoga. (55)
If Kuṇḍalinī ascends from her own place, then this one becomes liberated; if she does not leave her own place, then this one remains bound—thus he says: "The bulb," etc. (verse 55).
The Praṇava is the support of all:
these worlds—Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar—and their presiding deities, the Moon, the Sun, and Fire, abide within its measures; that supreme light is "Om."
That supreme light, which is "Om," is that wherein the three times, the three gods, the three worlds, the three vowels, and the three Vedas abide.
He states that the *praṇava* is the support of the worlds beginning with *bhūr*: "Bhūḥ," etc. (56–57).
Bondage and liberation arise from the movement and non-movement of the mind;
when the mind moves, there is saṃsāra, and when it is motionless, it is called liberation.
Therefore, one should stabilize the mind through supreme wisdom according to the prescribed method. (58)
The mind is the cause of all objects; when it exists, the three worlds exist. When it is extinguished, the world is extinguished; therefore, it must be treated with diligent effort. (59)

Since the movement and non-movement of the mind are the causes of bondage and liberation, one should reflect that the mind does not exist apart from oneself; thus he says: "In the mind. Because it is so, therefore [the following]. (58–59)
Through the contemplation that the mind is not distinct from its own self, there arises the direct realization of Brahman:
"I am the mind, having the form of the sky; I am the mind, facing in all directions.
I am the mind, and I am the Self; yet the mind is not the absolute Supreme. (60)
Mental actions arise from the mind; the mind is stained by sins.
But when the mind becomes transcendent (unmanī), there is neither merit nor sin.
When, by perceiving the mind with the mind, it becomes devoid of mental fluctuations,
then that supreme Brahman, which is so difficult to perceive, is seen.
Having perceived the mind with the mind, the knower of yoga becomes liberated;
having perceived the mind with the mind, one should always remember that which culminates in the state beyond mind (unmanī).
Having perceived the mind with the mind, one should always remain established in yoga;
having perceived the mind with the mind, it is seen through the ten causal conditions.
When the cognitive conditions are perceived, then one becomes a lord of yogis. || 65 ||
Bindu, nāda, kalā, jyotis, and abindu, as well as the polar star (dhruvatāraka),
that which is peaceful (śānta) and that which transcends it— that is called the Supreme Brahman.
But the mind is an obscuration to Brahman; when that mind is destroyed through its *sattva* aspect, Brahman shines forth—thus he says, "The mind.
When the mind has attained the state of the Lord of Pure *Sattva*, [it realizes]: "I am the mind, having the form of the sky."
Because of the absence of mental modifications such as volition (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth; for if the mind, when functioning as pure being (*sattva*), were Brahman, [the author] says:

"The mind is not the absolute Supreme" (60). But the mind characterized by the functions of *rajas* and *tamas* is merely the mind, from which actions arise. However, if one's mind should become *unmanī* (transcending the mind) [then it is otherwise]. (61)

Having perceived with a mind that has attained the state of *sattva* that the mind had fallen into states such as *tamas*, and having seen it as false, one becomes thus devoid of mental activity through such vision. || 62-63 ||

p. 461) For the yogin who remains after having perceived [the Self], a realization is seen through ten conditions—just as one who is informed, "You are the tenth," possesses the realization, "I am the tenth"—so too for one who is informed by "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), the realization "I am Brahman" (brahmāsmi) is seen. The sense is that the knowledge "I am Brahman" arises. || 64-65 ||

Regarding the question of what kind of Brahman has the sphere of conditions (*pratyaya-gocara*), it is described here as *bindu* and *nāda*. From the perspective of one's own ignorance (*svājñādi-dṛṣṭyā*), it appears in the form of *virāṭ* and so forth as the light of *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*. Because it is distinct from the ear and other senses, as well as from *virāṭ* and the rest, it is "without *bindu*" (*abindu*); it is the *otā* (the pervader), the polar star, the consciousness that is the permissive witness (*anujñātṛ-caitanya*).
Being itself eternally established with respect to its own function, it carries across the ocean of existence those who worship it;
it is the consciousness whose single flavor is the "permission" (anujñā), wherein the conceptualizations beginning with Virāṭ and ending with Anujñātṛ have subsided.
Beyond that, however, is the non-conceptual consciousness. That which shines forth in reality as everything from Bindu up to the limit beyond that [Anujña]—that is it.
Everything is said to be the Supreme Brahman.

The meaning is that its status as Brahman is absolute because it expands (bṛṃhaṇāt) by being established as its own non-dual nature alone, which is realized through the negation of all elements of duality—such as the bindu and other categories—that are distinct from itself. || 66 ||
The inseparable relationship between the vital breath and the mind is such that [the mind] laughs, exults, plays with delight, and rejoices;
it extends life through the intellect and fears danger from all sides. (67)
He is obstructed, awakened by grief, deluded by new prosperity, trembles at the deeds of his enemies, and rejoices laughing out of desire. (68)
Through mindfulness, one should recognize the mind that delights in desire within the body;
in whatever place the vital breath (vāyu) dwells, there the mind certainly dwells as well. (69)
The mind is said to be the moon, the sun, the wind, and sight;
O Brahmin, the drops (bindu), resonance (nāda), and the creative power (kalā) are the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
He says that whatever is to be contemplated beyond Brahman is the mind— thus, "it laughs" (verse 67–68).
In this way, by means of the recollection [of the process] beginning with laughter and ending with the dalliance of the god of love,
he states the inseparability of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*citta*)— thus, "where" (verse 69).

He describes the state of mind, vital breath, and vision as being the moon, sun, and fire, and the state of the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā* as being Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa, in the verse beginning with "manaḥ" (verse 70).
The continuous pursuit of the inner sound (nāda) is the cause for the dissolution of the mind;
through constant pursuit of the sound, latent impressions (vāsanā) become utterly exhausted.
O Lotus-born One, both the vital breath (marut) and the mind dissolve into the stainless state.
That which is indeed the resonance (nāda) is the drop (bindu), and that is proclaimed to be the mind (citta).
One should accomplish the unity of these three: resonance, the drop, and the mind. || 72 ||
The mind alone is indeed the drop (bindu), the cause of both origination and maintenance;
from the mind the drop arises, just as milk [contains] the nature of ghee.

Regarding the question, "What is the cause for the dissolution of the mind together with its latent impressions (vāsanā)?"—the answer is: "Always [in this state]. He states that at the very moment the latent impressions are exhausted, one should contemplate the unity of sound (nāda), the point (bindu), and the mind within the stainless [reality]: "That which... (yaḥ).
But how, then, is there oneness between the mind and the bindu? To this he says: "The mind... (verse 73).
The method for the practice of the vital breath joined with the mind:
having fully understood the six wheels, one should enter the mandala of bliss.
One should draw in the wind and likewise direct it upwards. (74)
One should practice with the wind, the drop, the wheel, and likewise the mind;
through this single concentration, yogis attain immortality.

He says "six," etc., to indicate that for the sake of dissolving the mind which is the cause of all misfortune, one must practice the control of the vital breath (pavana) joined with the mind, preceded by a thorough knowledge of the six chakras: "The circle of bliss shining within the Suṣumnā. At the very moment of the yogi’s samādhi, he has accomplished his purpose.
He says that they "come to be" by means of meditative concentration (samādhi). || 75 ||

(463) Without practice preceded by the teacher’s instruction, there is no arising of knowledge; just as fire situated within wood does not emerge without friction, so too the lamp of knowledge does not arise without the yoga of practice. (76)
Just as a lamp inside a jar does not shine outside, yet when that jar is broken, the flame of the lamp becomes manifest. (77)
One's own body is said to be the jar, for the living soul is indeed that state;
when [the jar] is broken by the words of the Guru, the knowledge of Brahman shines forth. (78)
Having obtained the Guru as their helmsman, they cross the ocean of worldly existence by means of the power of the latent impression of practice, using his words as a firm boat. (79)
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.

To the objection that knowledge does not arise without practice, he gives an answer with an illustration, beginning with "Just as" (76). Furthermore: "In the middle of a jar" (77). It was said "a jar," where the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative. For the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed that state [of Brahman], once the portions of the individual soul to be discarded have been removed.
Because it is that state; when one's own ignorance regarding that has been shattered by the guru’s words, it is equal [to liberation]. || 78 ||
The Teacher is like the helmsman, and this [Self] taught by Him is like the boat;

the virtuous, relying upon Him, cross the ocean of worldly existence—thus he says: "By the ear," etc. Simultaneously with the knowledge born from the grace of the Teacher through the Śruti, the disciples...
The meaning is that they attain liberation (kaivalya), characterized by abiding as Brahman alone, which is devoid of all counter-correlates. || 79 ||
The word *iti* signifies the conclusion of the sixth chapter; the word *upaniṣad*, however, signifies the conclusion of the entire treatise.
Thus ends the sixth chapter. The commentary on the Yogaśikhā Upaniṣad has been clearly written by Upadeśabrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra.
The commentary on the Śikhopaniṣad is recorded as consisting of seven hundred [verses].
Thus ends the commentary on the Yogaśikhā Upaniṣad, completing the sixty-third [treatise] in the venerable exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Īśa.
